title: Hay Description Specification
description: A structured data model for describing hay in a standardized, machine-readable format. Developed to improve clarity, consistency, and efficiency in how hay is characterized, traded, and analyzed-whether in domestic or international markets.
introduction:
Hay is a foundational agricultural commodity, essential to the nutrition of dairy and beef cattle, horses, goats, camels, sheep, and other animals. In the United States, hay ranks among the leading cash crops by annual sales value, alongside corn, wheat, and soybeans. Yet unlike those crops, hay is traded entirely on an over-the-counter basis-through peer-to-peer negotiation, dealers, or brokers- without common product definitions or standardized digital tools.
The hay market does not inherently require centralized exchanges to function well. But it does suffer from two critical deficiencies:
  1. Buyers and sellers struggle to find one another efficiently.
  2. There is limited electronic facilitation of trading, particularly in matching, documentation, and decision support.

These limitations stem in part from the lack of shared standards. Without consistent product descriptions or data conventions, hay listings and negotiations rely on informal descriptions, resulting in persistent mismatches in perceptions of quality, weak price signals, and high friction in trade. This hinders regional and global commerce, limits market transparency, and slows investment in modern tools for production, logistics, testing, and quality control.
Efforts to standardize hay go back more than a century. As recently as the late 19th century, centralized hay markets operated in cities such as Boston, Chicago, and San Francisco. Since then, producer groups, academic institutions, extension agencies, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture have all proposed grading systems. But none has achieved enduring, widespread adoption.
Several developments now offer new opportunities for progress:
  - Hay exports are growing, especially alfalfa, which now trades across borders under increasingly formalized standards.
  - Testing technologies have matured, including laboratory-based wet chemistry and NIR spectroscopy.
  - Digital tools and platforms are emerging, enabling traceability from field to bale.
  - Online infrastructure allows global coordination, opening the door for community-led standards and interoperability.

This document proposes a formal product definition for hay-a structured data model that captures economically salient characteristics in a consistent format. Such a definition supports better listings, search, comparison, and traceability. Over time, it may also surface replacements in market behavior that inform the development of accepted grading practices.
This specification is published by Lode, a platform for improving transparency and connectivity in agricultural commodities markets. To participate or provide feedback, contact us at [insert email address] or visit lode.global.
This is a working draft subject to field testing and stakeholder refinement.
Planned additions include:
  - A reference dataset of forage varieties, with identifiers and metadata.
  - A registry of forage analysis laboratories supporting the specified testing methods and protocols.

field_naming_conventions.summary: New field identifiers follow these conventions. Existing identifiers are preserved for compatibility, including documented legacy exceptions:
rules: Words separated by a single underscore (_)
No spaces, hyphens, slashes, or special characters
Scientific abbreviations normalized to lowercase (e.g., ph, ppm, tdn)
Units of measure placed at the end, separated by underscores (e.g., mcal_lb, percent_dm)

field_validation_conventions.identity: Use id as the canonical identifier. Accept name when reading legacy definitions without id. When both exist, they identify one field and must match exactly. Resolve fields within their section and parent component, not by flattening all identifiers into one global dictionary. Preserve existing spelling, punctuation, case, enum values, data types, and nesting when reading or writing this draft. Do not silently rename legacy identifiers or strip punctuation from enum values.
field_validation_conventions.presentation: Titles are display labels, not identifiers. Read definition for meaning; legacy description and details remain supporting documentation. A title or numeric identifier is not required to interpret an existing field. New enum entries should be plain YAML scalars without Markdown backticks or pipe-delimited alternatives. Existing malformed enum lists require explicit migration review; do not automatically split or clean them in stored records.
field_validation_conventions.constraints: Distinguish a declared constraint from typical or advisory values in prose. Typical ranges and cross-field consistency comments are not hard rejection limits. A structured valid_range, when present, uses inclusive finite numeric min and/or max bounds; min must not exceed max. Use it only with int or float. Missing bounds do not imply zero or an arbitrary maximum. Do not create a valid_range by extracting a typical range from a narrative definition. If structured constraints and prose disagree, report a specification defect for review rather than guessing precedence or silently altering the record.
field_validation_conventions.optionality: Absence of required does not itself introduce a new mandatory field. Existing explicit requirements in field or section guidance still apply. Omission means not reported; it is not equivalent to false, zero, unknown, an empty string, or an empty list. Do not introduce defaults when migrating records. Future conditional requirements must distinguish a true value from mere presence; a populated false boolean is not true.
field_validation_conventions.validation_scope: YAML parsing and structural checks validate the specification document. They do not certify hay records, analytical results, scientific plausibility, reference registry membership, or implementations. Existing partial-date conventions and multi-select declarations remain unchanged in this proposal. Known legacy naming and enum defects are tracked explicitly for later migration.

sections.title: Traceability
sections.description: This section captures whether the hay can be traced to a clearly defined production lot and whether formal identifiers exist that facilitate lot-level tracking, recall, or certification. Traceability is increasingly important in high-value or regulated markets, as it supports inventory segregation, quality assurance, documentation of origin, and post-sale issue resolution.

fields.definition:
Affirms whether the hay being described originates from a single, defined lot, harvested under uniform agronomic and environmental conditions. A lot is defined as "forage taken from the same farm, field, and cut under uniform conditions within a 48-hour time period," as described in Ball et al. (2001).
This designation supports clarity in nutritional representation, quality assessment, and logistical consistency.
notes: This field represents a binary value: `true` if traceable to a single, defined lot; `false` otherwise.
Common use in export markets and quality certification workflows.

fields.valid_values: free-text, max 100 characters
fields.definition:
This field allows the seller to assign an internal identifier to the lot from which the hay originated. It may reflect farm, field, cutting, or date conventions relevant to the seller's operation. Systems should enforce a character limit of 100 to ensure consistency and compatibility.
Internal lot identifiers do not need to conform to any industry standard but should be unique within the seller's system. They may be used for inventory management, customer reference, and traceability across quality or testing modules.
A structured block consisting of two related fields: an externally issued lot identifier and the name of the organization or program that issued it. Used for regulatory or certification purposes.

components.definition:
This field records the externally issued lot identifier assigned to the hay or forage lot by a regulatory, certifying, or export authority. Its meaning depends on the associated lot_identifier_external.issuer field, which specifies the issuing organization.
External lot identifiers may appear on documents such as:
  - Organic certificates (e.g., USDA NOP Lot #12345)
  - Phytosanitary inspection reports
  - Export documents or permits
  - Weed-free forage program tags or declarations

The value may include letters, numbers, or a combination thereof. Systems should enforce a maximum of 100 characters and preserve the identifier exactly as provided by the issuing body, including any dashes, slashes, or formatting symbols.
This field enhances traceability and may support validation workflows, especially in regulated or export-focused markets.

Identifies the organization or program that issued the external lot identifier.
Common issuers include:
  - USDA - e.g., for organic certification or phytosanitary control
  - CFIA - Canadian Food Inspection Agency
  - State agriculture department - e.g., for weed-free programs or grading systems
  - Export certification agency - country-of-destination compliance
  - Organic certifier - under USDA NOP or equivalent programs
  - Weed-free program - e.g., NAISMA-affiliated
  - Other - custom or less common issuers

This structure allows systems and reviewers to assess the origin and regulatory weight of the identifier and may support future API integrations or document uploads.

fields.definition:
Indicates whether the seller maintains a system (digital or physical) for mapping specific bales or sub-lots to field-level characteristics, such as GPS coordinates, yield zones, or harvest time blocks.
Such mapping enables greater traceability, enhances data resolution for quality control, and may support integration with field data platforms or precision agriculture systems.
This capability is optional but increasingly valuable in transparent or regulated feed markets.

fields.title: Source fields
fields.definition: Optional provenance identifying the production fields contributing to the hay described by this record. Use one entry for one field and separate entries for multiple fields. This collection may be partial; it is not a claim of complete origin coverage, allocation by field, or bale-level mapping.
fields.guidance: Omission or an empty list means no source-field details are supplied, not that the hay came from one field or that its origin is unknown. Include at least a nonblank name or identifier in each supplied entry. When supplied, the collection must be a list of objects; null is not an empty list. Omit unavailable components rather than supplying null or blank strings. Do not use empty objects or multi_field/multi-field sentinel values to represent multiple fields. A field name is a display label and need not be unique. Interpret an identifier only within its issuer or scope; without that context it is an unscoped source value and must not be treated as globally unique. Preserve identifiers exactly, including leading zeros, case, spaces, and punctuation. Do not merge entries solely because their names or unscoped identifiers match. No registry is required. Do not infer or overwrite hay_single_lot_traceable, lot identifiers, lot_mapping_field_to_bale_supported, or location summaries from this collection. Entry order conveys no priority or contribution share; no count limit is imposed. Preserve conflicting source reports for review. Existing records require no migration.

components.title: Field name
components.definition: Source-reported human-readable field name. A name alone is permitted; it does not identify a field uniquely across farms or reporting systems.

components.title: Field identifier
components.definition: Opaque source-issued identifier for this production field. Store as a string, preserving its exact spelling and formatting; do not coerce to a number or substitute a lot, farm, or bale identifier.

components.title: Field identifier scope
components.definition: Source-reported issuer or namespace in which field_identifier is meaningful, such as a farm's field register or a named mapping system and account. This is free text, not a controlled registry or a guarantee of uniqueness. Supply with an identifier where known; scope alone is not a field reference.

fields.title: Source-field list completeness
fields.definition: Optional source-reported assertion about whether source_fields lists all production fields contributing to the hay described by this record. complete means every contributing production field is represented; partial means at least one contributing production field is omitted. This describes list coverage, not contribution quantities, identifier verification, or bale-level traceability.
fields.guidance: Omit this field when completeness is not asserted or is unknown. Omission never means complete or partial and does not change existing records. Supply a nonempty source_fields list with either value. A declaration alongside an omitted or empty list is inconsistent; retain the reported values and flag them for review rather than filling, discarding, or rewriting either field. null, blank strings, and unknown are not declared values. Do not infer completeness from list length, names, identifier scope, lot flags, or mapping capability. A complete list can contain one or multiple fields and does not establish unique or verified identities. Reassess the assertion if the list or the hay represented by the record changes; do not copy it automatically to a blend, split, or new lot. Do not infer or overwrite hay_single_lot_traceable, lot identifiers, lot_mapping_field_to_bale_supported, or location summaries. This adds no allocation percentages or bale-to-field relationships. Older consumers must tolerate unknown optional fields to accept enriched records.

sections.guidance:
Traceability fields should be completed to the extent feasible. While not all buyers require formal lot tracking, inclusion of traceability data - especially internal and external identifiers - can streamline certification workflows, support inventory segregation, and build buyer confidence.
Systems should validate consistency between hay_single_lot_traceable and identifier fields and may allow optional linking to field- or bale-level metadata for advanced users.

sections.title: Stand Composition and Agronomic Characteristics
sections.description:
This section describes the planted forage stand-the biological and agronomic foundation of the hay crop. It includes the intended composition of plant varieties, their representation in the harvested hay, and related agronomic details such as establishment method, density, and maturity at harvest.
These fields support transparency around crop planning, species selection, and cultural practices, helping buyers assess the identity, uniformity, and development stage of the forage. The section also captures information relevant to quality, palatability, and intended use, and it helps agricultural professionals interpret how the hay's characteristics relate to field management decisions.

fields.definition:
This field expresses whether the grower intended to plant a mixed stand (polyculture) or a pure stand (monoculture) of forage species.
A value of `true` indicates the intention to grow a mix of species or varieties; a value of `false` indicates a monoculture was intended.
This field captures grower intent and does not reflect the final outcome, which may differ due to environmental or agronomic factors. For example, a grower may plant an alfalfa/timothy mix, but only the timothy survives to harvest. This field would still be `true`.
This field pairs with `forage_species_type`, which records the actual species composition of the forage at harvest, and with the `hay_variety_instances` group, which captures the grower's target and achieved representation of each variety.

This field describes the biological classification of the forage species present in the hay at harvest. It reflects the actual or observed composition, rather than the grower's original intention.
- `grass`: The hay consists primarily of grasses, such as bermudagrass or orchardgrass. - `legume`: The hay consists primarily of legumes, such as alfalfa or clover. - `grass/legume mix`: Both grasses and legumes are present in significant proportion. - `other`: The forage does not fit into the above categories (e.g., brassicas, forbs, or specialty hays).
This field supports downstream applications such as nutritional analysis, ration formulation, and marketing. It is best determined based on post-harvest visual inspection or lab analysis, and complements `stand_mixture_intended`.

fields.valid_values: positive integer (0 or greater)
fields.definition:
This field reports how many distinct forage varieties were identified in the actual harvested crop. It supports both marketing claims (e.g., "two-variety blend") and technical purposes, such as determining how many instances of a `forage_variety_component` block will be included in a structured message.
This field reflects actual harvest outcome, not grower intent. By contrast, `stand_mixture_intended` expresses whether the grower intended a mixed or pure sward. These two fields together help distinguish between intent and result.
In a pure crop, this field should take a value of `1`. In a mixed crop, this field should take a value of `2` or more. If no species or varieties can be positively identified, the value should be `0`, and the `forage_species_type` should be set to `unknown`.
System validations may check for consistency across `stand_mixture_intended`, `forage_variety_count`, and any listed `forage_variety_component` entries.

This block describes each intentionally planted forage variety in the hay sward. Pure (monoculture) hay includes one instance; mixed (polyculture) hay includes two or more.
Each entry should reflect the grower's intention, variety name, and estimated contribution to the harvested crop. This supports both agronomic analysis and marketplace transparency.
Use this block in combination with `forage_variety_count` and `stand_mixture_intended` to document crop composition and stand complexity.

components.valid_values: reference list of forage species, subspecies, or named varieties
components.definition:
Enter the full name of the forage variety, such as `Tifton 85 bermudagrass` or `Vernal alfalfa`. When possible, include binomial nomenclature, common name, and GMO status if known or relevant.
Standardizing variety names supports better market searchability, agronomic traceability, and nutrient expectation setting.

Captures the intended proportion of a given forage variety in the seed mix or planting strategy. Use whole-number ratios to reflect seeding intent. For example, if the mix was designed to be 3 parts orchardgrass and 1 part alfalfa, enter `3` for orchardgrass and `1` for alfalfa.
This is not a percentage and does not need to sum to 100 - it expresses relative ratios. Systems can calculate proportional percentages from totals.
Helps buyers and agronomists understand the seeding strategy, even when outcomes differ due to growing conditions or stand establishment issues.

Captures the observed contribution of this variety in the finished hay. Enter a whole number percentage (e.g., `65` for 65%), based on visual inspection, lab results, or grower knowledge.
This value reflects real-world outcome and may differ from `variety_representation_target` due to environmental or agronomic factors.
Total values across all components should sum to approximately 100%, with minor discrepancies acceptable for estimated inputs.

fields.definition:
Records the predominant maturity stage of the forage stand at the time of harvest. Maturity at harvest strongly influences forage quality, including digestibility, fiber content, and crude protein.
Use the appropriate maturity scale depending on the crop's dominant species type:

  - **Grass scale**: Used for species like bermudagrass, orchardgrass, or timothy.
  - **Alfalfa (legume) scale**: Used for alfalfa or clover-dominant stands.

Selection of the correct maturity stage helps buyers and nutritionists anticipate hay characteristics and plan optimal livestock feeding strategies.
Indicates the method used to establish the forage stand. Establishment method can affect plant density, weed suppression, and long-term stand performance.

fields.valid_values: YYYYMMDD format (allow 00 for unknown day or month)
fields.definition:
Records the date on which the forage stand was planted or sown.
If the exact day is unknown, use `00` in the day field. If both day and month are unknown, use `00` in both (e.g., `20240000`).
Example:
  - `20240400` -> planted in April 2024 (day unknown)
  - `20240000` -> planted sometime in 2024 (month and day unknown)
Qualitatively assesses the density of the forage stand at the time of harvest. Higher density can indicate better competition with weeds and improved yield.

fields.valid_values: non-negative integer (0 or greater)
fields.definition:
Records the number of years the current forage stand has been in place at the time of harvest. It reflects how long the same root system and plant population have been producing harvestable hay from the same field without replanting or reseeding.
Newly established stands may offer better vigor and fewer weeds, while older stands may show declining productivity, species composition shifts, or increased weed pressure.
Enter `0` if this is the first year of the stand's establishment. This field is especially important for perennial forages such as alfalfa, bermudagrass, or orchardgrass.

sections.title: Field Location and Growing Environment
sections.description:
This section describes the field location and environmental characteristics where the hay was produced. Geographic factors play a significant role in hay quality, influencing aspects such as nutrient content, texture, and palatability. Elevation, climate classification, and irrigation infrastructure all shape growing conditions and harvesting outcomes.
These fields support traceability, enable regional comparisons, and help buyers assess how site-specific factors may affect hay performance for their intended use.

fields.valid_values: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code (2-character string)
fields.definition:
Specifies the country in which the hay was produced, using the standardized ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code set. Examples include `US` for the United States, `CA` for Canada, and `MX` for Mexico.
Using this internationally recognized format allows for consistent and automated identification of national origin across systems and jurisdictions. This field supports traceability, compliance with import/export requirements, and transparency for buyers concerned with geographic sourcing.
System interfaces may implement dropdown menus or auto-complete fields linked to an official ISO 3166-1 code list to minimize input errors.

fields.valid_values: ISO 3166-2 subdivision code (e.g., US-TX, CA-ON)
fields.definition:
Specifies the first-level administrative region associated with the hay's origin, using the ISO 3166-2 code format. The full code typically includes the country code followed by a hyphen and a subdivision identifier (e.g., `US-TX` for Texas, United States).
Consistent use of ISO 3166-2 subdivision codes allows for clear geographic traceability and regional classification across jurisdictions. This field can be used for compliance tracking, climate zone mapping, and regional market analysis.
System interfaces may present filtered subdivision options once a country code is selected to reduce user input errors and improve usability.

fields.valid_values: free-text string, max 100 characters
fields.definition:
Records the county, parish, district, or other subnational jurisdiction in which the hay was grown. It provides more granular geographic detail than country or subdivision codes and may be important for local traceability, extension service classification, or compliance with region-specific programs.
Because standardized naming varies across countries and regions, this field is implemented as a free-text entry. However, systems may optionally use a lookup table or restrict input to known county names within the selected subdivision and country.
This field complements `hay_origin_country_code` and `hay_origin_subdivision_code` to form a complete geographic trace of the product's source.
Maximum character length: 100

fields.valid_values: postal or ZIP code, max 20 characters
fields.definition:
Captures the postal code (or ZIP code) for the location where the hay was grown. It offers a standardized method for identifying origin at a highly localized level and may support integration with mapping, logistics, or regional compliance systems.
Postal codes vary in format by country (e.g., `90210` in the U.S., `K1A 0B1` in Canada, `75008` in France). This field accepts any format valid in the associated `hay_origin_country_code`, up to 20 characters in total length.
Implementing systems may optionally validate against country-specific postal code replacements or offer auto-complete features based on the selected country and subdivision.
This field complements `hay_origin_country_code`, `hay_origin_subdivision_code`, and `hay_origin_county` for full geographic traceability.

fields.valid_values: positive or negative integer (interpreted via associated units field)
fields.definition:
Captures the elevation of the field in which the hay was grown.
Elevation can influence temperature, growing degree days, and forage composition. Higher elevations often correlate with lower lignin levels-resulting in softer, more palatable hay-making elevation an indirect but meaningful indicator of potential forage quality.
Enter a numeric value corresponding to the elevation of the field's center point, rounded to the nearest whole number. Use a negative integer if elevation is below sea level.
This field must be interpreted in conjunction with `source_field_elevation_units`, which indicates whether the value is measured in `meters` or `feet`.
Elevation data may be obtained from GPS tools, topographic maps, or online elevation services based on coordinates or postal code.

Specifies the unit of measurement used in the `source_field_elevation` field. Accurate unit identification is essential for interpreting elevation values correctly and ensuring consistent data across systems.
- `meters`: Elevation is expressed in meters above or below sea level. - `feet`: Elevation is expressed in feet above or below sea level.
When implementing this standard in software systems, consider validating elevation values for plausibility within the chosen unit. For example, elevations exceeding 9,000 meters or 30,000 feet may require review.
This field enables flexibility for global users who may record elevation data in different systems of measurement, while ensuring clarity for comparison and analysis.

fields.valid_values: Koppen-Geiger climate classification code (e.g., Cfa, BSk, Dfb)
fields.definition:
Records the generalized climate classification for the field where the hay was grown, using the Koppen-Geiger climate classification system.
Examples include:
  - `Cfa` - Humid subtropical (e.g., Southeastern United States)
  - `BSk` - Cold semi-arid (e.g., High Plains)
  - `Dfb` - Humid continental, warm summer (e.g., Northern Midwest)

Including this classification provides context about growing conditions such as temperature range, precipitation replacements, and seasonal variation. These factors can influence forage species selection, nutrient density, and cutting intervals.
System implementations may allow the user to select from a predefined list or map climate zones automatically based on location data. Values must conform to the standard Koppen-Geiger codes, typically in 2-3 letter formats.

fields.valid_values: positive decimal number
fields.definition:
Captures the size of the field or parcel from which the hay was harvested.
Field area is relevant for assessing yield per acre/hectare, validating production claims, and understanding the scale of the operation.
Values should be entered as positive decimal numbers. Round to the nearest `0.1` unit unless greater precision is available or required. For example, a field approximately twenty-two and a half acres would be recorded as `22.5`.
The appropriate unit of measure must be declared in the associated `source_field_area_units` field. If multiple fields contributed to the lot, enter the combined area. System interfaces may offer auto-calculation based on linked parcel data.

Specifies the unit of measurement used in the `source_field_area` field. Standardizing units ensures clarity in reporting and comparability across listings and geographies.
- `acres`: Commonly used in the United States and a few other countries. One acre equals 43,560 square feet
  or approximately 0.405 hectares.
- `hectares`: The standard metric unit of land area, equal to 10,000 square meters or approximately 2.471 acres.
Users should select the unit most appropriate for their region or reporting needs. System implementations may convert between units internally but should always preserve the original unit used for input and display.

Describes the general irrigation context in which the hay was grown:

  - `rainfed only`: Crop is typically grown without any irrigation; relies solely on rainfall.
  - `irrigation available`: Irrigation systems are available to supplement rainfall, but are not always necessary.
  - `irrigation required`: Reliable irrigation is essential for growing this hay crop in the region or operation.

This field offers buyers insight into crop reliability, regional water dependency, and resilience under dry conditions.

Indicates the primary irrigation method available to the producer:

  - `none`: No irrigation equipment or systems are available.
  - `flood`: Water is distributed by gravity over the field.
  - `sprinkler`: Water is applied using static or movable sprinkler systems.
  - `pivot`: A rotating center-pivot system is used to apply water in a circular replacement.
  - `drip`: Water is delivered directly to the root zone through emitters or tubing.

This field complements `irrigation_status` by describing technical capacity rather than agronomic necessity.
fields.validation_guidance:
These two fields describe related but distinct aspects of water management:

  - `irrigation_status` expresses the agronomic need or reliance on irrigation.
  - `irrigation_method_available` identifies what system or method is available, if any.

Suggested validation rules:
  - If `irrigation_status` is `rainfed only`, then `irrigation_method_available` should be `none`.
  - If `irrigation_status` is `irrigation required`, then `irrigation_method_available` must not be `none`.
  - If `irrigation_status` is `irrigation available`, then `irrigation_method_available` must not be `none`.

fields.definition:
Records the primary irrigation method actually used during the most recent production cycle of the hay crop:

  - `none`: No irrigation was applied; the crop was fully rainfed.
  - `flood`: Irrigation water was distributed by gravity flow across the soil surface.
  - `sprinkler`: Irrigation was applied using stationary or movable sprinklers.
  - `pivot`: A center-pivot system was used to irrigate the crop.
  - `drip`: Water was delivered directly to the root zone using drip lines or emitters.
  - `unknown`: The grower or seller does not know or did not report the irrigation method used.

This field complements `irrigation_method_available` by indicating which method was actually deployed. It helps assess water inputs, agronomic practices, and environmental conditions influencing the crop's growth and final quality.

sections.title: Soil and Field Management
sections.description:
This section captures how the grower prepares and maintains the soil to support a healthy forage stand. It includes information about fertilizer applications, soil amendments, and general nutrient management.
These practices influence crop yield, plant vigor, and nutritional quality of the harvested hay. They also help downstream users assess environmental practices, sustainability, and alignment with production goals (e.g., high-protein dairy forage vs. lower-input grazing hay).
Where applicable, fields differentiate between nutrient application to legume vs. grass crops- acknowledging, for example, that nitrogen is often unnecessary for legumes due to biological nitrogen fixation.

fields.valid_values: YYYYMMDD format (supports zero placeholders)
fields.definition:
Records the date of the most recent soil test used to guide nutrient and pH management decisions for the current hay crop.
Soil testing helps optimize fertilizer and lime application, supports environmental stewardship, and informs yield and quality expectations.
- Use `YYYYMMDD` for known full date - Use `YYYYMM00` if day is unknown - Use `YYYY0000` if both month and day are unknown - Use `00000000` if no soil test was conducted
This field enhances transparency and may support future traceability or certification requirements.

fields.valid_values: range from 4.5 to 8.5
fields.definition:
Records the pH of the soil based on the most recent test.
Soil pH affects nutrient availability, microbial activity, and crop performance. Most forage crops grow best in soils with a pH between 6.0 and 7.5, though legumes like alfalfa perform best when pH is above 6.5.
If this field is used, the value should reflect a recent, lab-confirmed test. Systems may prompt for this field only if `soil_tested_recently = true`.
Buyers and agronomists may use this value to evaluate crop suitability, field management, and potential nutrient deficiencies or toxicities.

Indicates whether agricultural lime or another pH-adjusting amendment was applied to the field prior to or during the hay crop cycle.
- `true`: Lime was applied - `false`: No lime was applied - `unknown`: The seller is unsure or has not tested the soil
Liming helps correct soil acidity and is particularly important for legumes like alfalfa, which require near-neutral pH for optimal growth.
Disclosing lime application supports transparency in soil fertility management and helps buyers understand underlying factors that may affect nutrient uptake and crop quality.

fields.valid_values: YYYYMMDD format (supports zero placeholders)
fields.definition:
Records the date on which lime was last applied to the field.
Lime affects soil pH gradually, so knowing the timing helps interpret its likely influence on the crop's root environment and nutrient uptake.
- Use the most recent date if lime was applied more than once - Use `YYYYMM00` or `YYYY0000` if the exact day or month is unknown
Systems may prompt for this field only if `lime_applied = true`.
This information supports traceability, fertility planning, and nutrient interaction modeling.

fields.valid_values: YYYYMMDD format (supports zero placeholders)
fields.definition:
Captures the most recent application date of nitrogen fertilizer for the hay crop.
Nitrogen fertilization is a key factor influencing crude protein levels, growth rate, and overall forage yield.
- Use `YYYYMMDD` for full date - Use `YYYYMM00` if day is unknown - Use `YYYY0000` if month and day are unknown - Use `00000000` if no nitrogen was applied
Timely disclosure of nitrogen use helps buyers assess nitrate risk and understand expected nutrient content.

fields.valid_values: YYYYMMDD format (supports zero placeholders)
fields.definition:
Indicates the most recent application date of potassium fertilizer.
Potassium supports plant water regulation, stress tolerance, and disease resistance - all of which influence forage quality and yield.
- Use `YYYYMMDD` for full date - Use `YYYYMM00` if day is unknown - Use `YYYY0000` if month and day are unknown - Use `00000000` if no potassium was applied
Disclosing potassium use assists in evaluating stand health and potential forage longevity.

fields.valid_values: YYYYMMDD format (supports zero placeholders)
fields.definition:
Documents the most recent application date of phosphorus fertilizer.
Phosphorus promotes root development, stand establishment, and early plant growth - critical for long-term forage productivity.
- Use `YYYYMMDD` for full date - Use `YYYYMM00` if day is unknown - Use `YYYY0000` if month and day are unknown - Use `00000000` if no phosphorus was applied
Understanding phosphorus usage helps evaluate early season vigor and nutrient management strategy.

fields.valid_values: non-negative integer
fields.definition:
Captures the quantity of nitrogen applied during the most recent fertilization event.
- Use whole numbers only. - Enter `0` if no nitrogen was applied.
This field must be interpreted in conjunction with `amount_fertilized_units`, which defines the unit of measure. Nitrogen influences plant growth, crude protein levels, and overall yield.

fields.valid_values: non-negative integer
fields.definition:
Specifies the quantity of potassium applied during the most recent fertilization event.
- Use whole numbers only. - Enter `0` if no potassium was applied.
Potassium enhances plant tolerance to drought and disease, supports stem strength, and improves forage quality. The applicable unit is defined in `amount_fertilized_units`.

fields.valid_values: non-negative integer
fields.definition:
Indicates the quantity of phosphorus applied during the most recent fertilization event.
- Use whole numbers only. - Enter `0` if no phosphorus was applied.
Phosphorus is vital for root development, energy transfer, and early-season growth in forage crops. This field should be interpreted in conjunction with `amount_fertilized_units`.

Specifies the unit of measure for the fertilizer quantity fields:

  - `amount_fertilized_nitrogen`
  - `amount_fertilized_potassium`
  - `amount_fertilized_phosphorus`

Choose only one unit system per entry, based on local or regulatory preference. For example, most U.S. producers will use `pounds per acre`, while metric-based countries will use `kilograms per hectare`.
Consistency in unit selection is required for accurate comparison and analysis.

A list of organic amendments applied to the soil. Each entry represents a separate application of compost, manure, crop residue, or similar material.
This information supports evaluation of nutrient management practices, sustainability, and long-term soil health strategies.

components.definition:
Identifies the type of organic material applied to the soil.
Use `other` if the amendment does not fit the listed categories and consider providing a supplemental explanation if needed.

Records the quantity of the amendment applied, rounded to the nearest whole number.
The unit of measure is defined separately in `amendment_amount_units`.

Defines the unit of measure used for reporting the amendment amount.
Choose the most appropriate based on how the amendment was applied or recorded.

Captures the date the amendment was applied.
This timing can influence nutrient availability, microbial activity, and the amendment's overall impact on the crop.
Use `00000000` if the date is unknown. Use `YYYYMM00` or `YYYY0000` for partial dates where day or month is unknown.

sections.title: Intended Use and Market Context
sections.description:
This section captures the grower's intended livestock audience, production philosophy (including certifications), and other contextual factors relevant to how the hay is positioned in the market.
These fields help buyers assess suitability for their specific animals, comply with regulatory or programmatic requirements (e.g., organic or weed-free sourcing), and identify potential constraints (e.g., GMO import restrictions).

fields.definition:
Identifies the primary intended animal class or application for which the hay or forage is marketed.
Improves alignment between buyer needs and product suitability by signaling expected quality standards, palatability, and feed safety requirements.
Valid values include:
  - `Dairy` - High-energy, high-protein, low-fiber forage suitable for lactating dairy cows
  - `Beef` - For growing, breeding, or finishing beef cattle with varied quality tolerance
  - `Horse` - Typically dust-free, low NSC forage with consistent texture and color
  - `Goat` - Moderate- to high-protein forage, tolerates stemmier material
  - `Sheep` - Requires attention to copper and energy levels; typically higher quality than beef forage
  - `Deer` - Highly digestible forage for farmed or captive cervids
  - `Camel` - Includes llamas, alpacas, and camels; suitable for coarser forage
  - `Rabbit` - High-fiber, low-calcium forage; typically small-stem grass hay
  - `Guinea pig` - Similar to rabbit requirements; may need stricter control on mold and texture
  - `Tortoise` - Drier, low-protein hays (e.g., timothy or orchardgrass)
  - `Zoo/Wildlife` - Regulated or specialized forage for zoological or rescue settings
  - `Landscape` - Erosion control, bedding, weed suppression, or decorative mulch
  - `Other` - Any unlisted use, including emerging or nontraditional forage markets

Whether this field is implemented as single- or multi-select should be determined by the platform.

Captures the functional purpose for which the hay was intended - such as maintaining body condition, supporting growth, or producing milk.
- `maintenance`: Intended for animals not in production (e.g., dry cows, idle horses). - `growth`: Designed to support young or growing animals. - `lactation`: Targeted for milk-producing animals with high energy/protein demand. - `work`: For animals performing physical labor (e.g., working horses). - `general purpose`: No specific function; applicable to various use cases. - `unknown`: Intention not known or disclosed.
This metadata helps buyers evaluate whether the hay aligns with their nutritional goals and may inform expected quality ranges.

Describes whether the hay was produced from a genetically modified crop and whether any non-GMO designation is formally certified.
- `GMO`: Hay was produced from a genetically modified crop (e.g., Roundup Ready alfalfa). - `non-GMO certified`: Hay was produced from a non-GMO crop and has been certified by a recognized
  non-GMO verification program.
- `non-GMO (uncertified)`: The producer affirms that the hay is non-GMO but without formal certification. - `unknown`: GMO status of the source crop is not known or not disclosed.
This field is important for export, specialty feed, and organic markets, where GMO crops may be restricted or excluded by regulation or buyer preference.
Examples of accepted non-GMO certification programs include:
  - Non-GMO Project Verified
  - USDA Organic (prohibits GMO use)
  - Certified Naturally Grown (if includes GMO-free attestation)
  - EU Organic Certification (Regulation (EU) 2018/848)

Notable regulatory contexts:
  - **European Union**: Requires GMO labeling above 0.9% content for feed products
  - **Mexico**: Imposes GMO corn restrictions with broader trade implications for GMO-related products

Accurate classification enhances transparency, supports marketing claims, and ensures regulatory compliance.

Captures the production-related certifications or designations that apply to the hay.
These certifications provide assurance to buyers about how the hay was grown and handled and may influence eligibility for certain markets or regulatory programs.
- `certified organic`: Certified under a recognized organic program (e.g., USDA NOP, EU Organic) - `certified non-GMO`: Certified free of genetically modified organisms - `certified weed free`: Certified noxious weed-free (often required for public land or export) - `transitional organic`: Produced using organic-compliant methods but not yet fully certified - `none`: No applicable production-related certifications - `unknown`: Certification status is not known or not disclosed
Multiple values may be selected for products that hold more than one certification (e.g., both `certified organic` and `certified weed free`).
System implementations should allow multi-select input and validate accordingly.

Captures the primary distribution context or market scope for which the hay was prepared.
This field may infer associated quality expectations, packaging format, and logistical considerations.
- `local`: Intended for use within the immediate community or county - `regional`: Distributed across a multi-county or state/province area - `national`: Distributed across the entire country - `export`: Intended for international sale or shipping - `unknown`: Not disclosed or not applicable
This field may support regulatory compliance (e.g., export documentation), freight planning, or market segmentation analysis.

Identifies the export-related documentation available for the hay.
Such documentation may be required by importing countries, states, or agencies to ensure compliance with quarantine laws, invasive species control, or import regulations.
Valid options include:
  - `phytosanitary certificate`: Verifies the hay is free from regulated pests and meets the
    import requirements of the destination country
  - `fumigation certificate`: Confirms the hay has been treated with a fumigant prior to shipment
  - `certificate of origin`: States the country of production, often required for trade preference or compliance
  - `weed-free declaration`: Indicates certification of noxious weed-free status under applicable standards
  - `none`: No export documentation is provided with this hay
  - `unknown`: The documentation status is not known or not disclosed

This field supports international trade, reduces risk of shipment rejection, and helps buyers comply with regulatory requirements in their jurisdiction.
Multiple values may be selected to reflect all relevant documentation.

sections.title: In-Season Crop Management
sections.description:
This section documents how the hay crop was managed during the growing season - including cutting strategy, weed and pest management, and other contextual information such as weather stresses or field notes.
These details help buyers and agronomists evaluate how active crop management may have influenced the resulting forage quality, consistency, and marketability.

fields.valid_values: free-text string, max 500 characters
fields.definition:
Optional field for describing notable growing conditions that may have impacted the hay crop - such as drought, flooding, hail, or heat stress.
Because such conditions are unpredictable and varied, this field uses a free-text format to allow flexible input.
Example entries:
  - `Light drought stress during early growth; recovered by late season`
  - `Localized hail damage in May`
  - `Flooded low areas did not contribute to harvest`

This field is optional but may support transparency in high-trust markets or export documentation.

Estimates the level of weed presence in the field during the growing season.
- `none`: No visible weed pressure; stand appears clean and uniform - `low`: Minor weed presence; unlikely to affect palatability or marketability - `moderate`: Noticeable weed presence; may influence feed value or buyer preference - `high`: Significant weed presence; likely to reduce market value or trigger restrictions - `unknown`: Seller does not know or declined to report
This field supports transparency and may inform eligibility for "certified weed free" programs.

Discloses whether herbicides were applied to the source field(s) during the growing season.
Herbicide use may influence weed pressure, forage purity, and chemical residue risk.
- `true`: Herbicides were used - `false`: No herbicides were applied - `unknown`: Seller does not know or does not wish to disclose

Reports the level of pest pressure during the growing season.
- `none`: No notable pest activity - `low`: Minor pest presence; little or no impact - `moderate`: Noticeable pest presence; some impact on leaf loss, yield, or quality - `high`: Major pest infestation likely to affect quality or marketability - `unknown`: Seller does not know or declined to report
Pests may include aphids, armyworms, leafhoppers, or weevils.

Discloses whether pesticides (excluding herbicides) such as insecticides, fungicides, or miticides were applied to the hay crop during its growing season.
This field is important for organic compliance, residue monitoring, and sensitive livestock species.
- `true`: One or more pesticide treatments were applied - `false`: No pesticide treatments were applied - `unknown`: Seller does not know or does not wish to disclose

Indicates whether a preservative - such as propionic acid - was applied to the hay during harvest or storage.
Preservatives are used to inhibit mold growth and improve storability for hay baled at higher moisture levels.
- `true`: A preservative was applied - `false`: No preservative was used - `unknown`: Seller does not know or does not wish to disclose

Indicates whether a coloring agent was applied to the hay for cosmetic or marketing purposes.
While coloring agents do not alter nutritional value, they may influence buyer perception or suitability for certain markets.
- `true`: A coloring agent was used - `false`: No coloring agent was applied - `unknown`: Seller does not know or does not wish to disclose

fields.valid_values: positive integer
fields.definition:
Represents the grower's customary number of hay cuttings per growing season, based on long-term practice with this stand or forage type.
This field supports agronomic profiling and helps buyers understand harvest frequency and regrowth potential.

Identifies the growth stage at which the grower typically aims to cut hay for optimal quality and yield.
- `early bud`: Alfalfa cut when first buds appear (dairy-grade forage) - `boot stage`: Grass cut when seed head is enclosed (balance yield and quality) - `full bloom`: Often cut here for seed production or low-cost forage - `other`: Atypical or user-defined cutting target - `unknown`: Not disclosed or unknown
This is a grower-reported target, not a measurement of actual maturity at harvest.

sections.title: Harvest-Level Data
sections.description:
This section documents key facts about the harvest event or events from which the hay was produced.
It includes cutting number, harvest dates, field yield, and average bale weight - along with indicators of harvest-specific practices such as conditioning.
These fields provide crucial context for traceability, logistics, and quality interpretation, especially when evaluating consistency across lots, seasons, or producers.
Accurate reporting of this data supports both market transparency and informed decision-making by buyers and nutritionists.

fields.valid_values: YYYYMMDD format (supports zero placeholders)
fields.definition:
Represents the commencement date of the hay harvest, typically corresponding to the mowing date.
This date informs the consumer about the age of the hay, its seasonal timing, and allows for correlation with local weather conditions.
Use the following placeholder format for unknown components:
  - `YYYYMMDD`: Full date known
  - `YYYYMM00`: Day unknown
  - `YYYY0000`: Month and day unknown

Estimations are allowed using zero placeholders as needed.

fields.valid_values: YYYYMMDD format (supports zero placeholders)
fields.definition:
Represents the conclusion date of the hay harvest.
This must not precede `harvest_date_start`.
If `hay_single_lot_traceable` is `true`, the time span from start to end must not exceed 48 hours.
Placeholder formats:
  - `YYYYMM00`: Day unknown
  - `YYYY0000`: Month and day unknown

fields.valid_values: non-negative integer
fields.definition:
Indicates which cutting (e.g., 1st, 2nd) of the season produced this hay.
Enter `0` if the cutting number is unknown.

fields.valid_values: decimal percentage (wet basis)
fields.definition:
Records the average hay moisture content at harvest, based on baler sensor data.
Values above ~18% may signal risk of spoilage without preservation treatment.
This field is optional.

fields.valid_values: decimal percentage (wet basis)
fields.definition:
Records the highest observed moisture value from baling equipment sensors.
Helps detect risk zones for mold or internal heating in storage.
Optional field, complements `baler_moisture_average`.

Indicates whether hay was mechanically conditioned (e.g., crimped or crushed) during harvest.
Conditioning accelerates drying and helps reduce nutrient loss from weathering.

fields.valid_values: positive integer
fields.definition:
Targeted average bale weight set on the baler or planned by the grower.
Must be interpreted with `bale_weight_units`.

fields.valid_values: positive integer
fields.definition:
Average weight of bales in the lot, measured or estimated.
Must match the units in `bale_weight_units`.
Interpretation depends on `bale_weight_assessment_method`.

Specifies the method used to determine reported bale weight.
Enables transparency for buyers and analysts.

fields.valid_values: positive integer
fields.definition:
Total number of bales produced for this hay lot.
Used to calculate inventory, shipping, and total yield.

fields.valid_values: whole number
fields.definition:
Total yield (mass) from the source field(s), calculated or estimated.
Must be interpreted with `source_field_yield_units`.

Unit of measure for `source_field_yield`.
Must align with the reported numeric value.
- Metric ton = 1,000 kg (~2,204.62 lbs) - British ton = 2,240 lbs - U.S. ton = 2,000 lbs

sections.title: Hay packaging
sections.description:
This section describes the physical form in which the hay is currently packaged for sale or shipment. It includes bale dimensions, binding material, compression method, and other packaging details that affect storage, transport, handling, and customer preferences.
Packaging specifications may differ from original harvest conditions - particularly in cases where hay has been rebaled or processed after the initial cutting. Buyers rely on this data to assess compatibility with feeding systems, freight capacity, and regulatory or market requirements.
Note: Some hay may be reprocessed or rebaled after the initial harvest. Fields in this section (including weight, shape, and compression) describe the hay as currently packaged for sale or shipment - which may differ from the original harvest form.
sections.guidance: Packaging fields use id as their canonical identifier. The matching name keys are retained as compatibility aliases for consumers of v0.91.1. Existing enum values remain unchanged. Omitted values mean not reported; omission must not be interpreted as false or as a measured zero. Numeric weights and dimensions must be finite and greater than zero. Do not impose typical commercial bale sizes as hard validation limits. Require bale_weight_units when any of bale_weight_intended, average_bale_weight, or bale_weight_intended_repackaged is populated. Require bale_dimension_units when any dimension is populated. Unit fields may be supplied before measurements are available. For rectangular bales, use length, width, and height. For round bales, use diameter and axis; width and height remain accepted legacy measurements under the conventions documented below. Do not derive a volume when shape, units, or the necessary dimensions are missing or ambiguous.

fields.name: hay_packaging_history
fields.title: Packaging history
fields.description: Describes whether the hay is in its original bale form or has undergone repackaging. Repackaging may include unrolling and re-baling, compressing for export, or resizing for specific markets.
fields.details:
- **original**: Hay is in the form in which it was first baled.
- **rebaled**: Hay was originally baled, then unrolled and baled again.
- **repackaged**: Hay was processed into a different format (e.g., compressed, shrink-wrapped).
- **unknown**: Packaging history is unclear or not disclosed.

This field supports traceability and helps buyers assess potential quality or handling concerns related to reprocessing.

fields.name: bale_weight_intended_repackaged
fields.title: Intended bale weight (repackaged)
fields.valid_values: A positive whole number representing the intended weight (in units defined by `bale_weight_units`) of each bale in its final, repackaged form.
fields.description: Applies only when hay has been re-baled or repackaged after the original harvest. This field specifies the target weight of the new bales, such as when large round bales are broken down and re-formed into smaller square bales.
fields.details:
This value is expressed in the same units as `bale_weight_units` (e.g., pounds or kilograms).
It reflects the intended packaging outcome and may differ substantially from the original `bale_weight_intended` captured at harvest.

Use this field only if `hay_packaging_history` includes values such as `rebaled` or `repackaged`.
When applicable, this field provides important clarity for buyers and logistics providers, especially in export or high-volume contexts.

System interfaces may optionally validate this field in relation to `bale_shape`, `bale_dimension_*`, or `bale_binding_material` fields to ensure internal consistency.

fields.name: bale_weight_units
fields.title: Bale weight units
fields.description: Specifies the unit of measurement used in `bale_weight_intended`, `average_bale_weight`, and `bale_weight_intended_repackaged`.
fields.details:
Most systems should standardize internally on one unit, but external presentation may vary by user preference or region.

Providing a clear unit prevents misinterpretation, especially when converting or comparing listings across geographies.

fields.name: bale_binding_material
fields.title: Bale binding material
fields.description: Records the primary material used to bind or wrap the bale for storage and handling.
fields.details:
Material type affects bale durability, safety, and disposal requirements.

- `twine`: Natural (e.g., sisal) or synthetic (e.g., polypropylene) twine.
- `net wrap`: Plastic or polymer netting, typically used on round bales.
- `wire`: Steel or galvanized wire, often used for high-density rectangular bales.
- `plastic strap`: Plastic strapping commonly used on compressed or export bales.
- `none`: No external binding applied to the bale.
- `unknown`: Binding material is not known or not disclosed.

fields.name: bale_binding_details
fields.title: Bale binding details
fields.description: Represents the bale's size and binding configuration. Independent of binding material.
fields.details:
This field captures the size, shape, and basic binding configuration of the bale. It is independent of the binding material (e.g., wire or twine), which is recorded separately in `bale_binding_material`.

- `small two-strand`: Small rectangular bale tied with two strands of twine or wire.
- `small three-strand`: Slightly larger small bale tied with three strands.
- `large 3x3x8`: Large square bale approximately 3'x3'x8'.
- `large 3x4x8`: Large square bale approximately 3'x4'x8'.
- `large 4x4x8`: Extra-large square bale approximately 4'x4'x8'.
- `round twine`: Round bale bound with twine.
- `round net wrap`: Round bale secured with net wrap.
- `round plastic wrap`: Round bale sealed in plastic, often for haylage.
- `other`: Non-standard or specialized bale types.

Binding material (twine, wire, net, plastic) should be separately recorded in `bale_binding_material`.

fields.name: hay_compression
fields.title: Hay compression level
fields.description: Represents the extent to which the hay bale has been mechanically compressed for storage or transport.
fields.details:
This field describes whether and to what extent the bale has been mechanically compressed to reduce its volume. Compressed hay is often produced for export or for storage efficiency.

- `standard`: Bales are not compressed beyond what occurs during baling.
- `mid-compressed`: Bales have undergone moderate compression (e.g., for container loading).
- `fully compressed`: Bales are significantly compressed using hydraulic or mechanical means.
- `unknown`: Compression status is not known or not disclosed.

This field is particularly useful in international trade and for evaluating bale density relative to storage or freight constraints.

fields.name: bale_shape
fields.title: Bale shape
fields.description: Represents the geometric shape of the hay bale.
fields.details:
This field records the geometric shape of the bale. Bale shape affects equipment compatibility, stacking, and handling procedures.

- `round`: Cylindrical bale shape, often larger and heavier.
- `rectangular`: Includes small square, mid-size, and large square bales.
- `other`: Includes cubes, wafers, or non-standard formats.

Shape selection may be influenced by market expectations, shipping constraints, or equipment availability.

fields.name: bale_dimension_width
fields.title: Bale dimension - width
fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the width of the bale, in the units specified by `bale_dimension_units`.
fields.description: Width of the bale, typically the short side of a rectangular face. For round bales, the legacy width value represents the diameter.
fields.details:
Enter the bale's width (short side of the rectangular face, or diameter for round bales).
Preserve the precision of the reported measurement; no fixed rounding is required.
For round bales, prefer bale_dimension_diameter. If width and diameter are
both supplied, they must describe the same diameter after unit conversion.

This field helps buyers assess compatibility with handling equipment and loading systems.

fields.name: bale_dimension_height
fields.title: Bale dimension - height
fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the height of the bale, in the units specified by `bale_dimension_units`.
fields.description: Height of a rectangular bale in its recorded storage or transport orientation. For round bales, this is a legacy measurement with unspecified orientation. It must not be assumed to represent either diameter or cylinder axis length.
fields.details:
Enter the rectangular bale height in its recorded orientation.
For new round-bale records, omit height and report bale_dimension_diameter
and bale_dimension_axis instead. Preserve height in historical records,
but do not copy it into either explicit field unless source documentation
identifies the measured direction. Do not infer that direction from equal
values, relative sizes, or the bale's current storage orientation.
A legacy height and an explicit axis may differ without a contradiction.
Preserve the precision of the reported measurement.

This field is important for planning stacking and clearance requirements in storage facilities.

fields.name: bale_dimension_length
fields.title: Bale dimension - length
fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the length of the bale, in the units specified by `bale_dimension_units`.
fields.description: Length of the bale, typically the longest axis for rectangular bales.
fields.details:
Enter the bale's length (longest axis for rectangular bales).
Preserve the precision of the reported measurement.

This measurement aids in evaluating stacking strategies and trailer fit.

fields.name: bale_dimension_diameter
fields.title: Bale dimension - diameter
fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the diameter of round bales, in the units specified by `bale_dimension_units`.
fields.description: Diameter of the bale, applicable only to round bales.
fields.details:
Use this field only for round bales. Enter the diameter of the cylinder,
preserving the precision of the reported measurement. For rectangular bales, leave this field blank
or exclude it from output.

Diameter is crucial for modeling bale volume and handling characteristics.

fields.title: Bale dimension - cylinder axis
fields.valid_values: finite decimal greater than zero
fields.definition: Length of a round bale along its cylinder axis, expressed in bale_dimension_units. Applicable only when bale_shape is round. This is independent of the bale's standing or lying orientation. Measure along the cylinder from one circular end face to the other; diameter is measured across a circular end face. Do not populate axis from legacy height or length without source confirmation of direction. Axis is not constrained to equal legacy height or diameter. Omit this field for rectangular or other bale shapes.

fields.name: bale_dimension_units
fields.title: Bale dimension units
fields.description: Unit of measurement used for all bale dimension fields.
fields.details:
This field specifies the unit of measurement used for the bale dimensions
listed above. Consistent units allow for accurate volume, storage, and logistics
calculations.

- inches: Common in North America for small bales.
- centimeters: Metric alternative to inches.
- feet: Common for large bales in U.S. agriculture.
- meters: Used in international and metric-based systems.

Implementing systems should support conversion and validation tools based on this field.

sections.title: Physical Characteristics and Condition
sections.description: This section captures the visible, tactile, and olfactory traits of the hay, as well as relevant effects from post-harvest weather exposure and storage-related degradation.

fields.definition:
Indicates whether the hay was exposed to rainfall while lying in the windrow (after mowing, before baling).
- `true`: Rainfall occurred during windrow stage - `false`: No rain fell on the hay while in windrow - `unknown`: Rain exposure is not known or not disclosed
Rain in the windrow can leach nutrients, promote mold, and reduce forage quality.

Indicates whether the hay was exposed to snowfall while lying in the windrow.
Snowfall can delay drying, increase moisture retention, and contribute to microbial degradation if the forage is not properly managed during the curing process.
Use:
  - `true` if snow fell on the hay while in the windrow
  - `false` if no snow was received during this stage
  - `unknown` if the seller is uncertain whether snowfall occurred

Snow exposure during curing is a key concern in colder climates and may influence storage recommendations and marketability.

Indicates whether the hay was exposed to sleet while lying in the windrow.
Sleet - a mix of rain and ice - can extend drying time, increase leaf loss, and accelerate physical weathering of forage material.
Use:
  - `true` if sleet fell on the hay during the windrow stage
  - `false` if no sleet occurred
  - `unknown` if the seller is uncertain whether sleet exposure took place

Even short periods of sleet can negatively affect hay quality, especially when followed by freezing conditions or prolonged curing.

Indicates whether the hay was exposed to hail while lying in the windrow.
Hail can physically damage forage by shattering leaves, bruising stems, or embedding ice into the material - all of which reduce forage quality and palatability.
Use:
  - `true` if hail fell on the hay during the windrow stage
  - `false` if no hail occurred
  - `unknown` if the seller is unsure about hail exposure

Even localized hail events can damage specific areas of a field. Sellers should respond based on the best available observation or weather data.

Indicates whether the hay was exposed to fog while lying in the windrow.
Fog can prolong moisture retention, delay drying, and increase the risk of mold growth or spontaneous heating - particularly if hay is baled before reaching safe moisture levels.
Use:
  - `true` if fog was observed or known to have affected the windrow
  - `false` if fog did not occur
  - `unknown` if the seller lacks information about fog exposure

Fog-related moisture is especially critical in humid climates or during short drying windows. Sellers should answer based on field observation or reliable local weather data.

Indicates whether the hay experienced heavy dewfall while lying in the windrow.
Dew can reintroduce moisture to partially dried forage, delaying curing and increasing the risk of microbial activity, mold development, or heat damage if the hay is baled prematurely.
Use:
  - `true` if significant dewfall was observed during the windrow stage
  - `false` if no heavy dew occurred
  - `unknown` if the seller lacks sufficient knowledge to assess dew exposure

Heavy dew is especially common under certain weather replacements or in specific regions. Accurate disclosure helps buyers assess quality risks related to post-mowing moisture events.

Seller's qualitative assessment of weather-related damage to the hay while it was lying in the windrow.
This field provides context for previously disclosed moisture events by allowing a summary-level judgment based on observation or experience.
Use:
  - `none` for no perceptible damage
  - `minor` for slight discoloration or nutrient loss
  - `modest` for moderate quality reduction
  - `substantial` for significant degradation in hay quality
  - `unknown` if the seller lacks enough information to assess

This qualitative field supplements binary moisture disclosures with human judgment, offering an important signal to buyers in the absence of lab analysis.

Indicates whether the hay received rainfall after it was baled.
Rainfall post-baling can introduce mold risk, lower palatability, and increase spoilage potential during storage.
Use:
  - `true` if the seller discloses that the hay received rainfall once baled
  - `false` if no rain fell on the bales
  - `unknown` if the seller has no knowledge of post-baling rain exposure

Accurate disclosure supports buyer decision-making and storage or feeding planning.

Indicates whether the hay received snowfall after it was baled.
Snow accumulation on baled hay can lead to external moisture exposure, spoilage, and mold growth - particularly during freeze-thaw cycles.
Use:
  - `true` if the seller discloses that snow fell on the bales after baling
  - `false` if no snowfall occurred
  - `unknown` if the seller lacks knowledge of post-baling snow exposure

Disclosure of snow exposure helps buyers assess potential quality degradation and storage-related risks.

Indicates whether the hay received sleet after it was baled.
Sleet exposure may cause surface moisture and freezing damage, compromising bale integrity, increasing spoilage risk, or complicating handling.
Use:
  - `true` if sleet fell on the hay after baling
  - `false` if no sleet occurred
  - `unknown` if the seller lacks knowledge of sleet exposure

Disclosure supports assessment of post-harvest vulnerability and product condition.

Indicates whether the hay received hail after it was baled.
Hail can damage the outer surfaces of bales, compromise structural integrity, and increase moisture penetration - all of which may lead to spoilage.
Use:
  - `true` if the hay was exposed to hail post-baling
  - `false` if no hail occurred
  - `unknown` if the seller is unsure about hail exposure

Although less common, hail can affect bale appearance, palatability, and storage performance.

Indicates whether the hay experienced excessive moisture after it was baled, such as fog, heavy dewfall, or condensation.
Use:
  - `true` if the seller discloses post-baling moisture exposure
  - `false` if no such moisture events occurred
  - `unknown` if the seller does not know or declined to report

Excessive post-baling moisture can lead to spoilage, mold, or bale heating - all of which may compromise hay safety, shelf life, or livestock health.

The seller's qualitative assessment of weather-related damage to the hay after it was baled. This summary includes deterioration from rain, snow, sleet, fog, dewfall, or other post-baling moisture events.
Valid values:
  - `None`: No known or suspected post-baling weather damage
  - `Minor`: Slight damage with minimal quality impact
  - `Modest`: Noticeable degradation affecting appearance or shelf life
  - `Substantial`: Significant degradation affecting usability or nutrition
  - `Unknown`: Seller is unable to assess damage severity

This field complements detailed weather exposure fields and supports transparency in product condition reporting.

A qualitative assessment of the leaf-to-stem ratio in the hay, based on visual observation or standard grading procedures. Leafiness is a key determinant of forage quality, as leaves generally contain more digestible nutrients than stems.
Classification scheme adapted from Bates (2007): - Very leafy: Dominated by leaves, minimal visible stem. - Leafy: Leafy with some stem presence. - Slightly stemmy: Noticeable stem content, but still a moderate leaf presence. - Stemmy: Predominantly stems, limited leaf material.
This field supports visual grading and may correlate with laboratory results for digestibility and nutrient density.

Captures a tactile assessment of the hay's texture, reflecting how soft or harsh it feels upon physical inspection. Texture can influence animal intake, particularly for selective livestock such as horses or young animals.
Classification follows the scheme from Bates (2007):
  - "Very soft and pliable": Tender and flexible, exhibiting no harshness.
  - Soft: Generally smooth with minor resistance to handling.
  - "Slightly harsh": Noticeable coarseness or rigidity.
  - "Harsh, brittle": Very coarse, easily broken, and may contain tough stems.

This qualitative measure complements analytical and visual data, aiding buyers in anticipating palatability and overall usability.

Records the dominant color of the hay at the time of sale, serving as a visual indicator of forage quality, harvest conditions, and storage practices.
Adapted from Bates (2007), the classification reflects common color categories:
  - "Natural green color of crop": Bright green, suggesting good curing and nutrient preservation.
  - "Light green": Slight fading due to sunlight exposure or aging.
  - "Yellow to slightly brownish": Indicates delayed harvest, aging, or weathering; potential nutrient loss.
  - "Brown or black": Often caused by rain damage, heating, or mold; may suggest spoilage or poor palatability.

Though subjective, hay color influences buyer perception and is frequently considered alongside laboratory analysis.

Captures the perceived odor of the hay as a sensory indicator of harvest and storage conditions. Adapted from Bates (2007), odor categories range from desirable to undesirable:

  - Clean--"crop smell": Fresh, sweet odor typical of well-cured hay.
  - Dusty: Dry, musty smell, possibly indicating excessive dust or aging.
  - Moldy: Clear mold odor, a sign of spoilage and potential health risk.
  - Somewhat sour: Mild fermentation scent, may reflect premature baling.
  - Sour: Strong sour odor due to improper curing or storage.
  - Rotten or otherwise foul: Foul smell from decay or contamination.

Odor assessments are subjective but critical for evaluating hay quality when lab data is unavailable.

Indicates whether visible mold is present on the hay, based on the seller's observation:

  - true: Seller affirms the presence of visible mold.
  - false: Seller affirms that no mold is visible.
  - unknown: Seller does not know or has not inspected closely enough.

Mold can lower forage quality, reduce palatability, and pose health risks- especially for horses and other sensitive animals. It may arise from excessive moisture, late baling, or poor storage conditions.

Indicates whether the hay is visibly dusty based on seller observation:

  - true: Seller affirms that visible dust is present.
  - false: Seller affirms that the hay is not dusty.
  - unknown: Seller does not know or has not assessed dustiness.

Dust may result from soil contamination, overly dry baling, or repeated handling. It can reduce palatability, pose respiratory risks to livestock, and lower visual appeal- making it an important indicator in quality assessments.

Indicates whether the hay exhibits visible or olfactory signs of rot based on seller observation:

  - true: Seller affirms that some or all of the hay is rotten.
  - false: Seller affirms that the hay shows no signs of rot.
  - unknown: Seller does not know or has not assessed whether the hay is rotten.

Rot may result from baling at excessive moisture, water damage, or poor storage. It can degrade nutritional quality and present health risks to livestock, making disclosure critical for transparency and quality assurance.

Indicates whether the hay contains visible weed material based on seller observation or knowledge:

  - true: Seller affirms that weed material is present.
  - false: Seller affirms that no weed material is present.
  - unknown: Seller is unsure or has not assessed for the presence of weeds.

Weeds may reduce nutritional value, harm palatability, or introduce invasive species. This field is especially relevant for export markets and buyers with strict feed quality standards.

Indicates whether burs-sharp, spiny plant structures-are present in the hay based on seller observation or knowledge:

  - true: Seller affirms that burs are present.
  - false: Seller affirms that no burs are present.
  - unknown: Seller is unsure or has not assessed for the presence of burs.

Burs may reduce hay desirability and pose risks to animals with sensitive mouths or coats, especially horses and show livestock.

Indicates whether insects or insect residues are present in the hay based on seller observation or knowledge:

  - true: Seller affirms that insects or insect remnants (e.g., wings, legs, webs) are present.
  - false: Seller affirms that no insect presence has been observed.
  - unknown: Seller is unsure or has not assessed for insect presence.

This information may influence buyer decisions related to cleanliness, palatability, and regulatory compliance, particularly for sensitive species or export markets.

valid_values: field | tarp-covered | open shed | enclosed barn | unknown
fields.definition:
Describes the most recent structure used to house or protect the hay before sale or pickup.
- `field`: Stored outdoors with no covering. - `tarp-covered`: Covered with tarp or plastic sheeting outdoors. - `open shed`: Stored under a roofed but open or partially enclosed structure. - `enclosed barn`: Stored in a fully enclosed building. - `unknown`: Final structure not known or not reported.
Describes the surface on which the bottom layer of bales was stored during the final storage stage.

valid_values: natural ventilation | forced ventilation | enclosed with limited airflow | unknown
fields.definition: Describes the airflow conditions in the final storage environment. Adequate airflow reduces spoilage risk.
Indicates whether the hay was restacked or relocated at any point after its original baling. Restacking may lead to leaf loss and nutrient degradation.
Indicates whether there are visible signs of moisture damage on any portion of the hay, such as mold, discoloration, or odor, during the final stage of storage prior to sale or transfer.

fields.valid_values:
A sequential list of storage and handling events from baling to sale. Each event may include:
- `location_type` (`string`): e.g., `farm`, `dealer yard`, `export staging` - `storage_structure` (`string`): e.g., `enclosed barn`, `tarp-covered` - `surface_type` (`string`): e.g., `pallets`, `ground`, `concrete` - `airflow_condition` (`string`): e.g., `natural ventilation`, `limited airflow` - `duration_estimate` (`string`): e.g., "10-15 days", "~1 month" - `restacked` (`boolean`): Whether the hay was restacked at this stage
fields.definition:
