Records a chronological sequence of handling or storage events for the hay from the time of baling through to its final location prior to sale or transfer.
This field supports enhanced traceability and allows buyers to assess how storage environments and handling practices may have influenced forage quality over time.
fields.guidance: Optional history in chronological order to the extent known. Preserve existing handling_events records and their free-text component values. Partial histories and an empty list are permitted; do not invent missing events, require a final stage, or impose a maximum number of events. Event labels are optional. If supplied, initial belongs on the first event, final on the last, with at most one of each. A single event may be labeled final; it need not also carry initial. Intermediate labels may repeat. Preserve legacy final_storage_structure, final_surface_type, final_airflow_condition, restacked_since_baling, and visible_moisture_damage independently. Do not synthesize, overwrite, or infer those summaries from an incomplete history. If summaries and events disagree, preserve both and flag the discrepancy for review. Their existing enums remain unchanged.

components.definition: Location category as reported, such as farm or dealer yard. Free text; no registry or fixed vocabulary is required.
Structure used during this event, such as enclosed barn or tarp-covered. Free text; do not copy into the legacy final summary without confirmation.
Surface under the hay during this event, such as pallets or ground. Free text.
Airflow during this event, such as natural ventilation or limited airflow. Free text.
Reported duration, including approximate expressions such as 10-15 days or ~1 month. Preserve uncertainty; do not convert to an exact duration.
Whether the hay was restacked during this event. Omission is not false and must not be inferred from an unknown history.
Optional initial, intermediate, or final label supplied by the source. Final means the final known event as of this record, not proof that delivery has occurred.
Optional list of source-reported visible degradation observations for this event. Use free-text entries; omission or an empty list does not prove that the hay was inspected or undamaged.

examples:
handling_events:
  - location_type: farm
    storage_structure: enclosed barn
    surface_type: pallets
    airflow_condition: natural ventilation
    duration_estimate: "30 days"
    restacked: false

  - location_type: broker yard
    storage_structure: tarp-covered
    surface_type: ground
    airflow_condition: enclosed with limited airflow
    duration_estimate: "10-15 days"
    restacked: true

sections.title: Nutrient analysis
sections.description:
This section captures laboratory test results and related metadata for the hay's nutritional profile. These metrics help buyers evaluate forage quality and suitability for various animal classes. When available, forage analysis results supplement visual observations and support data-driven ration formulation.
Fields cover whether the hay was tested, how the sample was processed, and selected analytical values.

fields.definition: Indicates whether a forage analysis has been performed on this hay. A value of `true` signifies that the hay has been tested through a lab or analytical facility. A value of `false` indicates that no testing has been done, while `unknown` allows for the possibility that the seller is unsure whether testing has occurred- e.g., in the case of a broker or distributor.

fields.valid_values: YYYYMMDD format
fields.definition:
Records the date on which the hay sample was collected for laboratory analysis. Accurate sample dating is important for interpreting results in the context of hay storage time, nutrient degradation, and marketing timelines.
Sampling should reflect the hay offered for sale and should be conducted using representative methods, such as a coring probe across multiple bales. Some laboratories require the sample date for regulatory or archival purposes.

Indicates whether the individual or entity that collected the hay sample was independent of the seller. A value of `true` denotes that the sample was taken by a third party, such as a certified lab technician or agricultural extension agent, with no financial interest in the sale of the hay.
A value of `false` indicates the sample was collected by the seller or someone affiliated with the seller. A value of `unknown` applies when the identity or affiliation of the sampler is not known.
This distinction may influence the buyer's confidence in the validity and impartiality of the analysis results, particularly in high-value transactions or formal feed programs.

Indicates whether the person who collected the hay sample holds a recognized certification in forage or feed sampling. A value of `true` means the sampler was certified by a qualified authority-such as a state agriculture department, accredited laboratory, or national hay testing council-at the time the sample was collected.
A value of `false` denotes that the sampler was not certified, while `unknown` applies when certification status is not known or not disclosed.
Certified sampling can improve the credibility and repeatability of forage analysis, especially in cases where sampling technique significantly influences test results.

Identifies the protocol used for collecting the hay sample.
A value of `NFTA` indicates the sample was collected according to guidelines established by the National Forage Testing Association (NFTA), which include specifications for core sampling depth, number of cores per lot, sampling equipment, and bale selection.
A value of `other` signifies that a different protocol was used-such as a custom, lab-specific, or industry-standard method outside NFTA guidelines. Users may wish to capture additional descriptive detail in a separate comments field if `other` is selected.
The sampling protocol can affect the reliability and comparability of analytical results and may be a key consideration in quality assurance or product claims.

Identifies the laboratory responsible for conducting the forage analysis. Accurate and transparent reporting of the testing laboratory helps ensure confidence in test results, supports traceability, and enables standardized reporting across producers and regions.
For external labs, the enumerated list should include commonly used, certified forage testing labs- many of which participate in the National Forage Testing Association (NFTA) proficiency program or equivalent international standards.
If analysis was conducted using in-house resources, enter `Internal lab`. It is advisable for sellers selecting this value to provide documentation of their testing procedures and equipment calibration where appropriate.

Identifies the analytical method used to evaluate the hay sample. This provides context for interpreting the precision and reliability of reported forage values.
- `Chemical analysis`: Traditional wet chemistry methods. Highly accurate and used to calibrate other methods. - `Near Infrared Reflectance (NIR) spectroscopy`: A rapid, cost-effective method that compares sample spectra
  to a calibrated database. Accuracy depends on sample type and calibration quality.
- `Both chemical analysis and NIR`: Both methods were applied to the same sample for validation or complementary
  results.

Understanding the method is essential for comparing results across samples and for evaluating suitability for ration formulation or regulatory compliance.

fields.valid_values: YYYYMMDD format
fields.definition:
Records the date on which the laboratory analysis of the hay sample was completed. This helps establish the timeline between harvest, sampling, and testing, which can influence interpretation of results- particularly for parameters sensitive to storage time (e.g., mold development or nutrient degradation).
Use the `YYYYMMDD` format. If the exact date is unknown, use `YYYYMM00` for unknown day or `YYYY0000` for unknown month and day.

fields.title: Laboratory sample identifier
fields.valid_values: free-text, max 100 characters
fields.definition: Identifier assigned by the testing laboratory to the sample whose results are reported. Preserve the identifier as issued, including leading zeros, punctuation, and case. Interpret it together with hay_testing_laboratory; sample identifiers are not assumed to be globally unique. Optional even when hay_tested is true, because historical reports may not disclose an identifier. Omit when unavailable; do not invent an identifier.

fields.title: Laboratory report reference
fields.valid_values: free-text, max 250 characters
fields.definition: Report identifier, file name, or URI identifying the original laboratory report supporting the analytical values. A URI is permitted but not required. Preserve the reference as issued. Availability of this field does not imply public access to the report or establish its authenticity. Optional; omit when unavailable.

fields.title: Laboratory sample preparation completed date
fields.valid_values: YYYYMMDD format (supports zero placeholders)
fields.definition: Date on which the laboratory completed sample preparation, such as drying, grinding, or homogenization, before analysis. Distinct from hay_sample_date (collection) and hay_testing_date (analysis completion). Use YYYYMMDD, YYYYMM00 for an unknown day, or YYYY0000 for an unknown month and day, consistent with existing analytical date fields. Omit when unknown; do not substitute a collection, analysis, or report issue date. Compare chronology only where the known date precision supports it.

fields.title: Laboratory processing notes
fields.valid_values: free-text, max 1000 characters
fields.definition: Laboratory-reported observations about preparation or handling of this sample, such as regrinding, moisture correction, or an unusual sample condition. Preserve source meaning and distinguish these notes from seller observations. Optional; omit when unavailable.

fields.title: Laboratory result qualifier
fields.valid_values: free-text, max 100 characters
fields.definition: Laboratory-issued code qualifying this report or sample's results, such as a rerun flag or a calibration warning. Preserve the code as issued and interpret it using the laboratory's report legend; codes are not assumed to be comparable across laboratories. This is not a hay grade, laboratory certification, or substitute for an individual analyte's result qualifier. Optional; omit when unavailable. Do not infer a passing result from omission.

fields.title: Laboratory moisture content
fields.definition: Water content of the laboratory sample as a percentage of its total as-received mass (wet basis). This is distinct from baler_moisture_average and baler_moisture_high, which describe sensor measurements during harvest. Optional even when hay_tested is true. Omit when unavailable; do not substitute a baler measurement or infer zero from omission.
fields.guidance: Preserve the laboratory-reported value and its precision. The 0 to 100 bounds express percentage arithmetic, not a commercial hay acceptance range. No typical moisture range is a hard rejection rule. Moisture and dry matter are complementary only for the same sample and measurement basis. An implementation may calculate a missing value as 100 minus its complement when those conditions are established, but must distinguish calculated results from laboratory-reported results in its own provenance. A calculated value must also satisfy the destination field's existing constraints; do not relax them or clamp a result. Never overwrite a reported value or compare unrelated samples. Review discrepancies allowing for reported rounding; this draft prescribes no universal equality tolerance.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the dry matter content as a percentage.
fields.definition:
Dry matter is the portion of the forage that remains after all moisture has been removed. It includes all nutrients - such as fiber, protein, minerals, and energy - and is the standard basis for comparing feeds and formulating rations.
This value is the mathematical complement of moisture content; that is, `dry matter = 100 - moisture content`. Most properly stored hay will contain 85% to 92% dry matter. Lower values may indicate elevated moisture and a risk of spoilage or heating during storage.
All nutrient values are typically reported on a dry matter basis to eliminate dilution effects from water and ensure comparability across feed types.
fields.guidance: This is the single specification definition of the existing dry_matter record key. Consolidating duplicate definitions does not create a new key, change stored values, or require a record migration. See moisture_content for same-sample and measurement-basis requirements before deriving a missing complementary result. Existing reported values remain authoritative.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the Relative Feed Value (RFV) of the hay sample.
fields.definition:
Relative Feed Value (RFV) is a standardized index used to estimate the overall quality of hay and other forages based on two key factors: digestibility and potential intake. It is calculated from Acid Detergent Fiber (ADF) and Neutral Detergent Fiber (NDF) values using the following formula:

  RFV = (Dry Matter Intake %) x (Digestible Dry Matter %) / 1.29

RFV is scaled such that full-bloom alfalfa has an index of 100. Higher values suggest improved animal performance due to better digestibility and intake. For example:

  - >150: Excellent
  - 125-150: Good
  - 103-124: Fair
  - 87-102: Poor
  - <87: Reject or very low quality

RFV does not account for fiber digestibility differences among forages and is gradually being replaced by Relative Forage Quality (RFQ) in many applications.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the Relative Forage Quality (RFQ) of the hay sample.
fields.definition:
Relative Forage Quality (RFQ) is an enhanced forage index that estimates overall feed value by incorporating both potential intake and fiber digestibility. It improves upon Relative Feed Value (RFV) by replacing Acid Detergent Fiber (ADF) with Total Digestible Nutrients (TDN) and factoring in Neutral Detergent Fiber Digestibility (NDFD), when available.
RFQ is calculated using formulas like:

  RFQ = (DMI, % of BW) x (TDN, % of DM) / 1.23

where:
  - DMI = Dry Matter Intake, based on NDF
  - TDN = Total Digestible Nutrients, based on ADF and NDFD

RFQ better reflects the true feeding value of forage for ruminants than RFV, especially for grasses, mixed forages, and those with high fiber digestibility. Like RFV, RFQ is scaled such that full-bloom alfalfa has a value of 100. For example:

  - >170: Prime
  - 150-170: Premium
  - 130-149: Good
  - 100-129: Fair
  - <100: Low quality

RFQ is now the preferred index in many extension and laboratory reports, particularly where NDFD is measured or predicted.

fields.valid_values: n/a
fields.definition: The NRC 2001 energy system provides detailed energy estimates used in ruminant nutrition modeling, particularly for dairy cattle. It is based on the 2001 National Research Council (NRC) guidelines and accounts for the dynamic digestibility of feeds, microbial protein synthesis, and nutrient availability. This model distinguishes among different energy values, each reflecting specific physiological processes and efficiencies.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the digestible energy (DE) of the hay sample in megacalories per pound (Mcal/lb), calculated at maintenance-level intake (1X). Typical values range from 0.85 to 1.25 Mcal/lb.
fields.definition:
Digestible Energy (DE) is an intermediate measure of forage energy content, calculated as the gross energy of the feed minus fecal energy losses. It is a precursor to metabolizable and net energy calculations.
This value is expressed in megacalories per pound of feed on a dry matter basis. The 1X designation refers to maintenance-level intake, which avoids energy-use adjustments for production (e.g., lactation or growth).
Typical DE values for hay range from 0.85 to 1.25 Mcal/lb, with higher values indicating better digestibility and energy availability. This field is used in ration formulation, particularly for horses, beef cattle, and sheep.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the metabolizable energy (ME) of the hay sample in megacalories per pound (Mcal/lb), calculated at maintenance-level intake (1X). Typical values range from 0.75 to 1.10 Mcal/lb.
fields.definition:
Metabolizable Energy (ME) is calculated as the Digestible Energy (DE) of the forage minus energy lost as gases (primarily methane) and in urine. It represents the portion of energy available for maintenance and production in the animal.
The 1X label refers to a baseline intake level (maintenance), meaning this energy value does not include intake adjustments for increased metabolic demand such as lactation or growth.
Typical forage ME values range from 0.75 to 1.10 Mcal/lb on a dry matter basis. This field is commonly used in ration formulation for ruminants and equines and serves as the foundation for calculating net energy values.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the net energy of lactation (NEL) of the hay sample in megacalories per pound (Mcal/lb), adjusted for intake at three times maintenance level (3X). Typical values range from 0.60 to 0.80 Mcal/lb.
fields.definition:
Net Energy of Lactation (NEL) estimates the energy available from forage for milk production after accounting for all energy losses - including fecal, urinary, gaseous, and heat increment. It is a critical measure in dairy cow rations.
The 3X designation reflects a standardized dry matter intake level that corresponds to three times the maintenance energy requirement. This intake level reflects typical consumption for lactating cows and improves comparability of NEL values across forages.
Values typically range from 0.60 to 0.80 Mcal/lb on a dry matter basis. This value is used extensively in balancing dairy rations and estimating milk yield potential.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the net energy available for maintenance (NEM) of the hay sample in megacalories per pound (Mcal/lb), assuming dry matter intake at three times maintenance level (3X). Typical values range from 0.50 to 0.75 Mcal/lb.
fields.definition:
Net Energy for Maintenance (NEM) is the portion of forage energy available to support the basic metabolic functions of livestock - such as body temperature regulation, organ function, and standing activity - without contributing to growth or production.
This value is calculated after subtracting all forms of energy loss, including fecal, urinary, gaseous, and heat increment losses. The 3X designation reflects intake level three times above basal maintenance, which aligns with standardized assumptions used in NRC 2001 energy modeling.
Typical hay samples range from 0.50 to 0.75 Mcal/lb NEM on a dry matter basis. Higher values indicate better-quality forage for maintaining body weight without needing energy supplementation.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the net energy for gain (NEG) of the hay sample in megacalories per pound (Mcal/lb), assuming dry matter intake at three times maintenance level (3X). Typical values range from 0.25 to 0.60 Mcal/lb.
fields.definition:
Net Energy for Gain (NEG) estimates the energy available for body weight gain - such as muscle and fat deposition - after an animal's maintenance requirements are met. It is particularly important for growing and finishing beef cattle and feedlot operations.
This value is expressed in megacalories per pound (Mcal/lb) of dry matter, with the 3X intake assumption standardizing the calculation across feeding models.
Higher NEG values are associated with higher-quality forages and support faster average daily gains (ADG). Typical hay samples fall between 0.25 and 0.60 Mcal/lb.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the digestible energy (DE) of the hay sample in megacalories per kilogram (Mcal/kg), calculated at maintenance-level intake (1X). Typical values range from 1.8 to 2.6 Mcal/kg.
fields.definition:
Digestible Energy (DE) measures the amount of energy in forage that is available to livestock after subtracting fecal losses from the gross energy content. This value is expressed here in Mcal/kg to support international and metric-based ration formulations.
The 1X designation indicates that the estimate is based on intake equivalent to one times maintenance energy requirement - a standard NRC basis. Typical DE values for hay range from 1.8 to 2.6 Mcal/kg on a dry matter basis.
While U.S. feeding systems often use Mcal/lb, metric values are common in international livestock nutrition contexts.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the metabolizable energy (ME) of the hay sample in megacalories per kilogram (Mcal/kg), calculated at maintenance-level intake (1X). Typical values range from 1.6 to 2.3 Mcal/kg.
fields.definition:
Metabolizable Energy (ME) is the amount of energy available to the animal after subtracting fecal, urinary, and gaseous losses from the Digestible Energy (DE) of the forage. This value is expressed in Mcal/kg to support metric feeding systems.
The 1X label signifies that the value is based on a dry matter intake equal to maintenance-level energy requirements. This is a standard assumption in NRC 2001 energy models for ruminants.
Most hays provide between 1.6 and 2.3 Mcal/kg of metabolizable energy on a dry matter basis. This value is essential for ration formulation, especially when comparing forage sources in metric-based nutrition models.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the net energy of lactation (NEL) of the hay sample in megacalories per kilogram (Mcal/kg), assuming dry matter intake at three times maintenance level (3X). Typical values range from 1.3 to 1.8 Mcal/kg.
fields.definition:
Net Energy for Lactation (NEL) represents the energy available from forage for milk production, after all losses from feces, urine, gas, and heat increment have been subtracted. This field expresses that value in Mcal/kg to support metric-based feed systems.
The 3X label reflects a standardized dry matter intake level equivalent to three times maintenance, in line with NRC 2001 energy modeling conventions. This assumption supports comparability of values across different forages and feeding scenarios.
Most hays fall between 1.3 and 1.8 Mcal/kg NEL on a dry matter basis. Higher values indicate improved energy density and are associated with earlier-cut or legume-rich forages suitable for lactating animals.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the net energy for maintenance (NEM) of the hay sample in megacalories per kilogram (Mcal/kg), assuming dry matter intake at three times maintenance level (3X). Typical values range from 1.1 to 1.6 Mcal/kg.
fields.definition:
Net Energy for Maintenance (NEM) is the portion of forage energy available to maintain essential animal functions such as thermoregulation, circulation, and tissue maintenance. It is a core energy metric in both beef and dairy nutrition models.
The 3X designation reflects dry matter intake at three times the maintenance requirement, following the standard intake assumption of the NRC 2001 model. This value is expressed in Mcal/kg to support international and metric-based nutrition systems.
Forage samples typically range from 1.1 to 1.6 Mcal/kg of NEM. Higher values indicate better energy efficiency for livestock maintenance needs, with legume and early-cut forages tending to score higher.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the net energy for gain (NEG) of the hay sample in megacalories per kilogram (Mcal/kg), assuming dry matter intake at three times maintenance level (3X). Typical values range from 0.55 to 1.3 Mcal/kg.
fields.definition:
Net Energy for Gain (NEG) estimates the amount of energy available in forage for supporting body weight gain - including muscle and fat deposition - after an animal's maintenance needs are met.
This value is reported in Mcal/kg on a dry matter basis, aligning with metric-based nutrition systems. The 3X intake label conforms to NRC 2001 energy modeling, assuming animals are consuming dry matter at three times their maintenance requirement.
Most forages range between 0.55 and 1.3 Mcal/kg NEG. Higher values correspond to higher energy-density hays and support greater average daily gains (ADG), especially in growing and finishing cattle.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the Total Digestible Nutrients (TDN) of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter, at maintenance-level intake (1X). Typical values range from 50.0% to 70.0%.
fields.definition:
Total Digestible Nutrients (TDN) is an estimate of the total amount of digestible fiber, protein, lipid, and carbohydrate in a forage. It serves as a key indicator of the forage's overall energy content.
The 1X designation indicates that the TDN value is calculated at an intake level equal to one times the animal's maintenance requirement. This is standard for NRC 2001 models and serves as the baseline for comparing forages.
TDN is expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Most hays range from 50% (low-quality grass) to 70% (high-quality legume). Higher TDN values indicate greater energy availability and generally correlate with earlier harvest maturity and better digestibility.

fields.valid_values: n/a
fields.definition:
This section contains total crude protein and various protein fractions as defined by forage testing laboratories and ruminant nutrition models. Protein fractions reflect how nitrogen is partitioned in the forage and influence how protein is degraded, absorbed, and utilized in the animal's digestive system.
The values in this section are particularly important when balancing rations for dairy and beef cattle using the NRC 2001 or CNCPS (Cornell Net Carbohydrate and Protein System) models.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the crude protein (CP) content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Typical values range from 6.0% to 25.0%.
fields.definition:
Crude Protein (CP) is an estimate of the total protein content in forage, calculated by measuring the nitrogen content and multiplying by a factor of 6.25. This includes both true protein and non-protein nitrogen (NPN) compounds.
Crude protein is expressed on a dry matter basis to eliminate dilution by moisture. Most grass hays contain 6%-12% CP, while legume hays (such as alfalfa) may contain 15%-25% CP, depending on maturity and harvest conditions.
CP is a standard input for animal ration formulation and is used to evaluate whether a forage meets the protein requirements of different livestock classes.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the available protein content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Typical values range from 5.0% to 22.0%.
fields.definition:
Available protein is the portion of crude protein (CP) that remains digestible and usable by the animal after accounting for reductions due to heat damage, insolubility, and fiber-bound nitrogen. It reflects the true nutritional value of the protein in the forage.
This value is often calculated as:

  Available Protein = Crude Protein - Acid Detergent Insoluble Crude Protein (ADF-CP)

Available protein is particularly important when evaluating hays that have been exposed to moisture during harvest or that may have undergone Maillard reactions (browning) due to overheating in storage.
Values are expressed on a dry matter basis. Legumes tend to have higher available protein content than grasses, and well-preserved hay will typically retain most of its crude protein as available protein.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the acid detergent insoluble crude protein (ADF-CP) content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Typical values range from 0.3% to 5.0%.
fields.definition:
Acid Detergent Insoluble Crude Protein (ADF-CP) is the fraction of crude protein that is bound to indigestible fiber components in the forage and is considered largely unavailable to ruminants. This includes protein that has been rendered inaccessible due to heat damage during harvest or storage.
ADF-CP is a key factor in calculating available_protein:

  Available Protein = Crude Protein - ADF-CP

Higher ADF-CP values typically indicate poorer forage quality. Values above 3.0% suggest significant heat damage or poor harvest conditions, and forages with high ADF-CP may underperform despite high crude protein content.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the adjusted crude protein (ACP) content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Typical values range from 5.0% to 22.0%.
fields.definition:
Adjusted Crude Protein (ACP) represents the total protein content of the forage after correcting for indigestible fractions, such as heat-damaged or fiber-bound protein. It provides a more realistic estimate of protein availability for livestock.
ACP is typically calculated as:

  Adjusted Crude Protein = Crude Protein - ADF-CP (or other unavailable protein fractions)

This field may overlap conceptually with available_protein, depending on how the lab or model calculates each. In your data model, this field can be retained to preserve compatibility with test results from labs that report both.
Values are expressed on a dry matter basis. Accurate representation of ACP is critical in formulating protein-sufficient diets, especially when working with weather-damaged hay.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the soluble protein fraction of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of crude protein (% of CP). Typical values range from 15.0% to 40.0%.
fields.definition:
Soluble Protein is the portion of crude protein (CP) that dissolves rapidly in rumen fluid and is quickly available for microbial fermentation. It includes non-protein nitrogen (NPN), peptides, amino acids, and some true protein.
This value is expressed as a percentage of the forage's total crude protein. A typical range for hay is 15%-40% of CP, with higher values indicating faster ruminal degradation and potentially greater risk of nitrogen imbalance if not matched with available energy.
Soluble protein is a component of degradable protein and is often used in formulating balanced rations for optimal microbial protein synthesis.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the degradable crude protein content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of crude protein (% of CP). Typical values range from 30.0% to 80.0%.
fields.definition:
Degradable Protein (also known as Ruminally Degradable Protein or RDP) refers to the fraction of crude protein that is broken down by rumen microbes into ammonia, peptides, and amino acids. This component supports microbial protein synthesis and overall fermentation efficiency.
This value is expressed as a percentage of the forage's total crude protein. It includes soluble protein as a subset, along with slowly degradable true protein fractions.
Values typically range from 30%-80% of CP. Forages with excessive degradability may require supplementation with rumen undegradable protein (RUP) to balance nitrogen supply with energy availability.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the neutral detergent insoluble crude protein (NDICP) content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Typical values range from 1.0% to 6.0%.
fields.definition:
Neutral Detergent Insoluble Crude Protein (NDICP) refers to the fraction of forage protein that is insoluble in the neutral detergent solution used to measure fiber (NDF). It is associated with the cell wall and may be partially or fully indigestible depending on forage quality and animal passage rate.
NDICP is typically larger than ADF-CP, as it includes both indigestible and potentially digestible fiber-bound protein. It plays a role in estimating the rumen undegradable protein (RUP) and metabolizable protein supply.
Values are expressed on a dry matter basis. High NDICP may indicate fiber maturity, weather damage, or overmature forage.

fields.valid_values: n/a
fields.definition:
This section includes individual amino acid concentrations in forage, typically expressed as a percentage of dry matter or as a percentage of crude protein. Amino acids are the building blocks of protein and play essential roles in growth, reproduction, and immune function in livestock.
While total protein content is often used in ration formulation, specific amino acid values-especially for lysine and methionine-are critical for precision feeding in dairy, swine, and poultry systems. These metrics are increasingly reported by advanced forage labs and integrated into metabolizable protein models.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the lysine content of the forage sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Values typically range between 0.1 and 3.0.
fields.definition:
Lysine is an essential amino acid required for growth, milk production, and muscle development. This field reports the lysine content of the hay sample on a dry matter basis. Results are typically derived from laboratory analysis and may vary based on forage type and maturity.
Values may be estimated via Near Infrared Reflectance (NIR) or measured via wet chemistry. For most hay samples, lysine content will fall within a typical range of 0.3% to 1.5% of dry matter.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the methionine content of the forage sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Values typically range between 0.1 and 0.5.
fields.definition:
Methionine is an essential amino acid involved in protein synthesis and methylation processes. It is particularly important for dairy animals and poultry. This field reports the methionine content of the hay sample on a dry matter basis, as determined by laboratory analysis.
Values are commonly derived from Near Infrared Reflectance (NIR) estimates or direct wet chemistry testing. Typical methionine levels in legume or grass hay range from 0.1% to 0.4% of dry matter.

fields.valid_values: n/a
fields.definition:
This section includes carbohydrate-related metrics that describe the fermentable energy potential of forage, including structural and non-structural fractions. Carbohydrates are the primary source of energy in ruminant diets and influence feed intake, fiber digestibility, and microbial protein synthesis.
Structural carbohydrates (e.g., NDF and ADF) affect rumen fill and chewing activity, while non-structural carbohydrates (e.g., sugars and starch) are rapidly fermentable and drive energy supply. These values are essential for evaluating forage quality and balancing rations under the NRC 2001 or CNCPS models.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the acid detergent fiber (ADF) content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Values typically range from 20.0 to 45.0.
fields.definition:
Acid Detergent Fiber (ADF) represents the fraction of forage composed of cellulose and lignin - the least digestible plant components. It is an important indicator of forage quality and directly correlates with digestibility. As ADF increases, digestibility decreases.
This value is expressed as a percentage of dry matter and is typically determined by laboratory analysis using either wet chemistry or NIR methods.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the neutral detergent fiber (NDF) content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Values typically range from 30.0 to 70.0.
fields.definition:
Neutral Detergent Fiber (NDF) quantifies the total cell wall content of forage - including hemicellulose, cellulose, and lignin. It is a key determinant of forage bulk and limits dry matter intake, especially in ruminants.
This field expresses NDF as a percentage of dry matter, and it is typically determined through laboratory analysis via NIR spectroscopy or wet chemistry. Lower NDF is generally associated with higher quality and palatability.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the lignin content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Values typically range from 2.0 to 12.0.
fields.definition:
Lignin is a complex, indigestible polymer found in plant cell walls. Its concentration significantly influences forage digestibility. As lignin content increases, the digestibility of both cellulose and hemicellulose declines.
This field expresses lignin as a percentage of dry matter. It is typically measured through laboratory analysis, with values varying depending on forage maturity, plant species, and environmental conditions.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the non-fiber carbohydrate (NFC) content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Values typically range from 20.0 to 45.0.
fields.definition:
Non-Fiber Carbohydrates (NFC) represent the portion of forage that consists of sugars, starches, pectins, and organic acids. These components are highly digestible and contribute significantly to the energy value of the forage, particularly in ruminant diets.
NFC is typically calculated using the formula:
  NFC = 100 - (NDF + CP + Fat + Ash)

This value is expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Forages with high NFC values provide more rapidly fermentable carbohydrates, which can be beneficial or risky depending on the animal class and overall diet formulation.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the starch content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Values typically range from 0.0 to 40.0, depending on forage type.
fields.definition:
Starch is a non-structural carbohydrate that contributes substantially to the energy density of a forage. It is highly fermentable in the rumen and often derived from grain content or immature plant material in mixed forages.
This value is expressed as a percentage of dry matter and is determined through laboratory analysis, typically via wet chemistry or NIR. While starch content is usually low in grass and legume hays, it may be higher in small grain or mixed forages harvested at the boot or dough stage.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the water-soluble carbohydrate (WSC) content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Values typically range from 2.0 to 20.0.
fields.definition:
Water Soluble Carbohydrates (WSC) include sugars and other carbohydrates that dissolve in water and are rapidly fermentable. These carbohydrates affect both the palatability of the forage and its fermentation characteristics when ensiled.
WSC is expressed as a percentage of dry matter. It is an important metric for animals sensitive to carbohydrate load - such as horses at risk of laminitis. It also plays a role in forage selection for high-energy diets or fermentation profiles.
Values are typically determined via laboratory analysis using wet chemistry methods.

fields.valid_values: n/a
fields.definition:
This section describes the ether-extractable fat content of forage, which includes fatty acids, oils, waxes, and other lipid-soluble compounds. While fat is a minor component of most hays, it contributes to the overall energy value of the forage and can affect digestibility, palatability, and feed stability.
Fat content is typically expressed as a percentage of dry matter and is measured using ether extraction methods. This value is used in ration balancing, particularly for high-producing animals and when evaluating forage blends or byproducts with higher lipid content.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the crude fat content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Values typically range from 1.0 to 5.0, though higher values may occur in certain treated or ensiled forages.
fields.definition:
Crude fat represents the ether-extractable portion of the forage sample, including lipids, fatty acids, waxes, and other ether-soluble compounds. While forage is not typically high in fat, this metric contributes to overall energy calculations.
Crude fat is expressed as a percentage of dry matter and is typically determined through laboratory extraction methods. Higher crude fat values may indicate the presence of oilseed additives or ensiled materials with higher lipid content.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the total fatty acid content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Values typically range from 0.8 to 3.5.
fields.definition:
Total Fatty Acids (TFA) represent the portion of ether-extractable material in forage that consists specifically of true fatty acids. This field excludes waxes, pigments, and other non-nutritive ether solubles included in crude fat.
TFA is a more precise indicator of a forage's energy potential and is commonly used in dairy ration models to estimate Net Energy of Lactation (NEL), Maintenance (NEM), and Gain (NEG).
This value is expressed as a percentage of dry matter and is typically estimated using chemical extraction techniques or derived from crude fat values using a standard coefficient (e.g., 0.8 x crude fat).

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the rumen unsaturated fatty acid load (RUFAL) of the hay sample, expressed in grams per kilogram of forage dry matter. Values for hay typically range from 2.0 to 10.0, though higher values may be seen in oil-rich or ensiled forages.
fields.definition:
Rumen Unsaturated Fatty Acid Load (RUFAL) is a calculated value representing the concentration of unsaturated fatty acids that can impact rumen fermentation. High RUFAL levels are associated with an increased risk of milk fat depression (MFD) in dairy cattle due to altered rumen biohydrogenation pathways.
This value is expressed in grams per kilogram of dry matter and is typically calculated from detailed fatty acid profiles. While forages generally have lower RUFAL values compared to byproduct feeds or oilseeds, some high-fat or ensiled hays may exceed typical levels.
Monitoring RUFAL is essential in balanced ration formulation for lactating cows, especially when multiple feed components contribute to total dietary fat.

fields.valid_values: n/a
fields.definition:
This section contains metrics that estimate the digestibility of forage and its contribution to usable energy in the animal. These values are critical for predicting animal performance, ration balancing, and evaluating forage quality over time.
Digestibility metrics may be based on laboratory analysis (in vitro or in situ), chemical composition, or predictive models such as NRC 2001 or CNCPS. Key values include in vitro digestibility, total digestible nutrients (TDN), and rates or extents of fiber digestion.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the in vitro true digestibility of the hay sample after 30 hours of fermentation, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Values typically range from 50.0 to 90.0.
fields.definition:
This field represents In Vitro True Digestibility (IVTD) at 30 hours, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. It reflects the proportion of the forage that is truly digestible by ruminants, based on simulated fermentation in a laboratory setting.
Higher values indicate better forage quality and higher energy availability. IVTD is typically determined using rumen fluid or enzymatic simulations and is often used as a benchmark for comparing the feeding value of different hay types.
This metric is particularly important for dairy and beef producers seeking to optimize forage efficiency and milk/meat production per unit of feed intake.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the 30-hour in vitro digestibility of the neutral detergent fiber (NDF) portion of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of NDF. Values typically range from 30.0 to 70.0.
fields.definition:
This field measures Neutral Detergent Fiber Digestibility (NDFD) after 30 hours of fermentation, expressed as a percentage of the total NDF content in the forage sample. It indicates how much of the fiber fraction can be digested by ruminants within a biologically relevant timeframe.
Higher values correspond to more digestible fiber and are associated with improved feed efficiency and animal performance. This value is especially important in dairy nutrition models such as those used by the NRC and CNCPS.
NDFD30 is typically measured through laboratory simulation using rumen fluid or enzymatic methods.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the rate of digestion (kd) of the forage sample, expressed in percent per hour. Values typically range from 2.0 to 8.0.
fields.definition:
The kd value represents the fractional rate at which forage dry matter or fiber is digested in the rumen. It is expressed as a percentage of the component digested per hour (%/hr). This parameter is used in dynamic ruminant models to estimate forage retention time and nutrient availability.
Higher kd values reflect faster digestion, typically associated with younger, more digestible forages. Lower values may indicate mature, weathered, or highly lignified material. Most kd values for NDF digestion fall between 2.0 and 8.0 %/hr.
Measured values are usually determined in vitro via rumen fluid incubation, or estimated via NIR calibration curves.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the total digestible nutrients (TDN) of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Values typically range from 45.0 to 75.0.
fields.definition:
Total Digestible Nutrients (TDN) is an aggregate energy metric that estimates the total amount of digestible material in a forage sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. TDN includes digestible fiber, crude protein, non-fiber carbohydrates, and fat (multiplied by 2.25).
TDN is a standard value in forage analysis reports and is used extensively in ruminant nutrition modeling. Higher TDN values indicate higher energy content and generally higher forage quality. Values vary based on forage species, maturity, harvest conditions, and preservation method.
TDN may be estimated from lab-measured nutrient fractions or predicted via Near Infrared Reflectance Spectroscopy (NIR).

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the digestible energy (DE) of the hay sample for horses, expressed in megacalories per pound of dry matter. Values typically range from 0.80 to 1.20.
fields.definition:
This field represents the Digestible Energy (DE) content of the hay sample for horses, expressed in megacalories per pound of dry matter. DE is the standard energy unit used in equine ration formulation and represents the amount of energy available to the horse after losses in feces are accounted for.
Typical values vary by forage type and maturity. Grass hays generally range from 0.80 to 1.00 Mcal/lb, while high-quality alfalfa can reach 1.15 Mcal/lb or more. This field may be calculated from lab-measured nutrient fractions (e.g., TDN or NDF) or derived from empirical models for horse digestion.
This value is useful for formulating diets based on energy requirements by class (maintenance, growth, lactation, work).

fields.valid_values: n/a
fields.definition:
This section includes macro- and micromineral concentrations in forage, typically expressed as a percentage or parts per million (ppm) of dry matter. Mineral content affects animal growth, reproduction, milk production, immune function, and feed efficiency.
Accurate mineral profiling is essential for identifying imbalances, preventing deficiencies or toxicities, and formulating balanced rations. Values may be measured directly via wet chemistry or estimated using Near Infrared Reflectance Spectroscopy (NIR) where calibrated.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the ash content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Values typically range from 6.0 to 12.0, with higher values indicating potential soil contamination.
fields.definition:
Ash is the total mineral residue remaining after complete combustion of a forage sample. It includes both essential macro- and microminerals, as well as any inorganic material introduced during harvest, such as dirt or sand.
This field is expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Ash levels above 12-14% are often considered abnormally high and may suggest soil contamination due to improper raking or baling from muddy fields.
Ash values are important for both mineral balancing and energy calculations, as high ash reduces the organic matter portion of forage and thus its true energy density.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the calcium content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Typical values range from 0.25 to 0.60 for grass hay and from 1.20 to 2.00 for legume hay.
fields.definition:
Calcium (Ca) is an essential macromineral required for bone development, muscle contraction, nerve function, and milk production. Forage calcium content varies widely based on plant species, growth stage, and fertilization practices.
Grass hays - such as bermudagrass, timothy, or orchardgrass - typically contain between 0.25% and 0.60% calcium on a dry matter basis.
Legume hays - such as alfalfa or clover - generally contain much higher levels, ranging from 1.20% to 2.00% calcium on a dry matter basis.
This value is typically determined through wet chemistry or NIR estimation. Accurate calcium values are essential in formulating balanced rations for dairy cattle, horses, goats, and other livestock, especially for preventing conditions such as hypocalcemia or milk fever.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the phosphorus content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Typical values range from 0.15 to 0.35 for grass hay and from 0.25 to 0.45 for legume hay.
fields.definition:
Phosphorus (P) is a macromineral that plays vital roles in skeletal health, energy metabolism, and reproductive function. It also supports microbial growth in the rumen, which is essential for digestion of fibrous feeds.
Grass hays generally contain between 0.15% and 0.35% phosphorus, depending on maturity, soil fertility, and harvest timing. Legume hays typically provide higher levels, ranging from 0.25% to 0.45%.
Forage phosphorus deficiencies are common in certain regions and must be corrected through mineral supplementation. The calcium-to-phosphorus ratio is also an important consideration in ration formulation, especially for growing livestock and equine diets.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the magnesium content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Typical values range from 0.10 to 0.25 for grass hay and from 0.20 to 0.40 for legume hay.
fields.definition:
Magnesium (Mg) is an essential macromineral involved in neuromuscular function, energy metabolism, and bone formation. In ruminants, magnesium deficiencies can lead to grass tetany (hypomagnesemia), particularly in fast-growing spring grasses with high potassium levels.
Grass hays typically contain between 0.10% and 0.25% magnesium, while legume hays - such as alfalfa - generally contain 0.20% to 0.40%.
This value is expressed as a percentage of dry matter and is usually measured by laboratory wet chemistry or estimated by NIR. Monitoring magnesium is important in mineral balancing, especially when potassium or nitrogen fertilization is high.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the potassium content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Typical values range from 1.00 to 3.00 for grass hay and from 2.00 to 3.50 for legume hay.
fields.definition:
Potassium (K) is an essential macromineral involved in fluid balance, muscle and nerve function, and plant health. While vital, excessive potassium in forage can impair absorption of magnesium and calcium in ruminants, contributing to conditions such as grass tetany and milk fever.
Grass hays generally contain between 1.00% and 3.00% potassium. Legume hays - especially when heavily fertilized - often range from 2.00% to 3.50%.
Potassium levels above 3.00% may require dietary adjustment or supplementation of other minerals to ensure metabolic balance, particularly in periparturient dairy cows or spring-calving beef herds.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the sulfur content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Typical values range from 0.10 to 0.25 for grass hay and from 0.20 to 0.35 for legume hay. Values above 0.40% may pose a risk of toxicity.
fields.definition:
Sulfur (S) is an essential mineral used in the synthesis of sulfur-containing amino acids and the production of B-vitamins by rumen microbes. It supports structural tissue development, including wool, hair, and hooves.
Grass hays generally contain 0.10% to 0.25% sulfur, while legume hays may range from 0.20% to 0.35%. Excess sulfur - particularly when combined with high-sulfur water or distillers grains - can cause neurologic disorders such as polioencephalomalacia (PEM) in cattle and sheep.
This value is expressed as a percentage of dry matter and is important when formulating rations for confined livestock, especially in high-performance beef and dairy systems.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the chloride ion (Cl-) content of the hay sample, expressed as a percentage of dry matter. Typical values range from 0.20 to 0.50. Values above 0.60% may indicate contamination or unusual environmental exposure.
fields.definition:
Chloride (Cl-) is a negatively charged electrolyte that contributes to acid-base balance, osmoregulation, and hydrochloric acid production in the digestive tract. In forage analysis, chloride is typically expressed as a percentage of dry matter.
Chloride is particularly important in dairy nutrition for calculating the Dietary Cation-Anion Difference (DCAD), which influences calcium metabolism and the risk of milk fever. Forages with high chloride concentrations are often used in close-up rations to promote a mild metabolic acidosis.
Most hays contain between 0.20% and 0.50% chloride. Concentrations above 0.60% are uncommon and may result from exposure to salt-rich water, coastal spray, or chloride-containing fertilizers.

fields.valid_values: A positive integer representing the iron content of the hay sample in parts per million (PPM). Typical values range from 100 to 500 PPM; values above 1,000 PPM may interfere with absorption of other trace minerals.
fields.definition:
Iron (Fe) is a trace mineral required for oxygen transport, enzyme systems, and immune function. It is generally abundant in forages and deficiency is rare. However, high iron levels - especially when combined with iron-rich water or supplements - can lead to reduced absorption of copper, zinc, and manganese.
Forage iron is measured in parts per million (PPM) on a dry matter basis. Most hays contain between 100 and 500 PPM iron. Levels above 1,000 PPM may result from soil contamination or iron-rich irrigation water and may require attention to overall mineral balance.

fields.valid_values: A positive integer representing the zinc content of the hay sample in parts per million (PPM). Typical values range from 20 to 50 PPM; values below 30 PPM may indicate marginal zinc availability.
fields.definition:
Zinc (Zn) is an essential trace mineral involved in enzyme function, immune response, wound healing, and reproductive performance. Forage zinc levels are commonly marginal or deficient, especially in high-calcium or high-iron environments where mineral interactions reduce bioavailability.
Zinc is reported in parts per million (PPM) on a dry matter basis. Most forages fall between 20 and 50 PPM. Levels below 30 PPM may be inadequate for optimal livestock performance and often require supplementation.
Monitoring zinc is especially important in young growing animals, breeding stock, and high-producing dairy cows.

fields.valid_values: A positive integer representing the copper content of the hay sample in parts per million (PPM). Typical values range from 5 to 15 PPM; values below 8 PPM may be marginal, while values above 20 PPM may pose toxicity risk, particularly in sheep.
fields.definition:
Copper (Cu) is an essential trace mineral involved in enzyme activity, immune function, connective tissue formation, and pigment synthesis. Copper deficiency is one of the most common trace mineral issues in forage-fed livestock, particularly in areas with high soil iron, sulfur, or molybdenum.
Forage copper is reported in parts per million (PPM) on a dry matter basis. Most hays contain between 5 and 15 PPM. Levels below 8 PPM are often considered marginal and may require supplementation. However, levels above 20 PPM can be toxic to sheep and should be evaluated carefully for species-specific feeding.
Mineral interactions should be considered when interpreting forage copper values. Supplemental copper should be based on total dietary antagonistic load, not forage concentration alone.

fields.valid_values: A positive integer representing the manganese content of the hay sample in parts per million (PPM). Typical values range from 40 to 300 PPM. Values below 40 PPM may be inadequate; values above 400 PPM are uncommon but generally not toxic.
fields.definition:
Manganese (Mn) is a trace mineral critical for skeletal development, reproductive health, and antioxidant enzyme function. Although many forages contain high levels of manganese, its bioavailability is low, and absorption is further reduced by high iron or calcium levels in the diet.
Forage manganese is measured in parts per million (PPM) on a dry matter basis. Most hays contain between 40 and 300 PPM. Levels below 40 PPM may warrant supplementation in growing or breeding animals, particularly when forage iron is elevated.
There is low risk of toxicity, even at elevated forage manganese levels, though excessive Mn can contribute to mineral imbalances. Forage analysis should be considered alongside total dietary load and antagonist levels.

fields.valid_values: A positive decimal value representing the molybdenum content of the hay sample in parts per million (PPM). Typical values are less than 2.0 PPM; values above 3.0 PPM may antagonize copper absorption in ruminants.
fields.definition:
Molybdenum (Mo) is a trace mineral required in very small amounts for enzyme activity in livestock. However, excess molybdenum can form thiomolybdate compounds in the rumen, which bind to copper and inhibit its absorption, leading to secondary copper deficiency.
Forage molybdenum is reported in parts per million (PPM) on a dry matter basis. Most forages contain less than 2.0 PPM. Concentrations above 3.0 PPM - especially when sulfur is also elevated - may contribute to copper antagonism. Values above 5.0 PPM are generally considered high risk for ruminants, particularly cattle and sheep.
This field is important for diagnosing trace mineral imbalances and planning appropriate supplementation strategies. When molybdenum levels are elevated, especially in combination with high sulfur, it may be necessary to increase dietary copper or use chelated mineral forms to ensure adequate absorption.

subsections.title: Acknowledgements

While the final structure and content reflect the judgment of the authors, the following contributors and sources provided invaluable perspective, data, and expertise throughout its development.
items:
County extension agents across Texas, Kentucky, New Mexico, and California who provided field-level insight
into hay production practices and buyer needs.
University faculty and forage specialists whose published research and personal correspondence
shaped key definitions and data models.
Hay testing laboratories and forage analysis professionals whose sample reports and reference values
guided the formation of nutrient analysis and traceability fields.
Ranchers, hay producers, merchants, and buyers who reviewed early drafts and offered practical feedback
based on real-world use cases and market conditions.
Members of the National Forage Testing Association (NFTA) and American Forage and Grassland Council (AFGC)
for their standards, publications, and advocacy for consistent forage quality reporting.
